lessons.title: Plants eat sunlight
body: Plants make their own food. They use sunlight to do it.
Most vegetables need lots of sun. Six hours a day or more is best.
Watch your garden for one day. See where the sun shines the longest. That is the best spot for tomatoes and peppers.
lessons.tip: Leafy plants like lettuce can grow with a little less sun.

quiz.q: How many hours of sun do most vegetables like?

sources.t: USDA Misc. Pub. 483, Victory Gardens (1943, public domain)

lessons.title: Water deep, not every day
body: Roots drink water from the soil.
A big drink once or twice a week is better than a tiny sip every day. Deep water helps roots grow long and strong.
Push your finger into the soil. If it is dry down to your knuckle, it is time to water.
lessons.tip: Water in the morning so leaves can dry in the sun.

quiz.q: How can you tell if the soil needs water?
options: Push your finger in the soil

sources.t: Univ. of Illinois Extension — When and How to Take a Soil Test

lessons.title: Soil is alive
body: Good soil is full of tiny living things. Worms, bugs, and fungi live there.
They break down old leaves into food for plants.
Dark, crumbly soil that smells sweet is healthy soil.
lessons.tip: Worms are great helpers. If you find many worms, your soil is doing well.

quiz.q: What do worms do for soil?

sources.t: USDA Misc. Pub. 483, Victory Gardens (1943, public domain)

lessons.title: How deep to plant a seed
body: A seed has a baby plant and a snack inside it.
A simple rule: plant a seed about two times as deep as it is wide.
Tiny seeds, like lettuce, go just under the soil. Big seeds, like beans, go deeper.
lessons.tip: Keep the soil damp until the seeds sprout.

quiz.q: How deep should you plant a seed?
options: About 2 times as deep as the seed is wide

sources.t: Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331 — Vegetable Planting Guide

lessons.title: What is frost?
body: Frost is ice that forms on cold nights.
Some plants, like tomatoes and basil, die in frost. Other plants, like kale and peas, do not mind the cold.
Your garden page shows your frost dates. Plant warm plants after the last frost in spring.
lessons.tip: If frost is coming, cover tender plants with an old sheet at night.

quiz.q: Which plant does NOT like frost?

sources.t: USDA Misc. Pub. 483, Victory Gardens (1943, public domain)

lessons.title: Mulch is a blanket for soil
body: Mulch is a layer of straw, leaves, or wood chips on top of the soil.
It keeps the soil wet longer. It keeps weeds from growing. It keeps roots cool in summer.
Put mulch around plants, but not touching the stems.
lessons.tip: Fallen leaves make free mulch.

quiz.q: What does mulch do?
options: Keeps soil wet and stops weeds

sources.t: USDA Misc. Pub. 483, Victory Gardens (1943, public domain)

lessons.title: Pull weeds when they are small
body: Weeds are plants growing where we do not want them.
They take water and food from your vegetables.
Small weeds are easy to pull. Pull them after a rain when the soil is soft.
lessons.tip: Ten minutes of weeding each week stops a big weed jungle later.

quiz.q: When is weeding easiest?
options: When weeds are taller than you

sources.t: Purdue Extension E-65 — Vegetable Insect Identification
NC State Extension — Insect and Related Pests of Vegetables

lessons.title: Good bugs and bad bugs
body: Not all bugs are bad. Ladybugs eat aphids. Bees carry pollen so we get fruit.
Some bugs, like hornworms, eat our plants.
Look under leaves often. Catch problems early and write them in your Pests log.
lessons.tip: Flowers like dill and marigolds invite good bugs to your garden.

quiz.q: Which bug helps your garden by eating aphids?

sources.t: USDA Misc. Pub. 483, Victory Gardens (1943, public domain)

lessons.title: Pick often to get more
body: Many plants make more food when you pick it.
Beans, zucchini, and cucumbers grow fast. Pick them while they are small and tender.
Write what you pick in your Yields log. Next year you can see if you grew more.
lessons.tip: Pick in the cool morning for the crunchiest veggies.

quiz.q: What happens when you pick beans often?

sources.t: Univ. of Missouri Extension G6203 — Common Diseases in the Home Garden

lessons.title: Move plants each year
body: Plants in the same family get the same bugs and sickness.
Tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes are one family.
Plant them in a different bed next year. This is called crop rotation. Your Plantings page helps you remember.
lessons.tip: Beans and peas add food to the soil. Plant hungry crops there next year.

quiz.q: Why do we move plant families to a new bed each year?

lessons.title: Give seedlings room

sources.t: USDA Misc. Pub. 483, Victory Gardens (1943, public domain)

body: Tiny seeds like carrots and spinach are sown thick, because some seeds do not sprout.
When the baby plants come up, pull out the extras. This is called thinning. Now the rest have room to grow big.
Bean and pea seeds are different. Plant them where you want them to grow and do not thin them.
lessons.tip: Snip extra seedlings with scissors so you do not pull up their neighbors.

quiz.q: Why do we thin carrot seedlings?
options: So the others have room to grow

lessons.title: Victory Gardens

sources.t: USDA Misc. Pub. 483, Victory Gardens (1943, public domain)
How to Grow a Victory Garden (1942, public domain)

body: A long time ago, during World War II, millions of families grew "Victory Gardens."
They grew food at home so there was more food for everyone. Kids helped too!
Their garden books said: pick a sunny spot close to home, away from big trees. That is still great advice today.
lessons.tip: A garden near your door gets more care, because you see it every day.

quiz.q: Where did Victory Garden books say to put a garden?
options: In a sunny spot near home

lessons.title: How to take a soil test

sources.t: Univ. of Illinois Extension — When and How to Take a Soil Test

body: Soil fertility, pH, and even structure change over time as crops use nutrients. Testing every 3–5 years tells you what your soil actually needs, so you do not waste money on the wrong fertilizer.
Fall is a good time: the soil is still above 50 °F, the season is winding down, and anything you add has time to break down before spring.
Use a clean trowel or probe. Take several small samples from across the bed, mix them in a clean bucket, and send about a cup of the mix to the lab. Test beds you treat differently separately.
A standard test reports pH, phosphorus, potassium, organic matter, and some micronutrients. Many labs can test for lead on request — worth doing near old houses or roads.
lessons.tip: Log your results under Soil & fertilizer so you can compare tests across years.

quiz.q: How often does Illinois Extension suggest testing garden soil?

sources.t: Univ. of Illinois Extension — When and How to Take a Soil Test

lessons.title: Reading N-P-K on fertilizer
body: Every fertilizer bag shows three numbers, like 5-10-5. They are the percent of Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), and Potassium (K).
Nitrogen grows leaves and stems. Phosphorus helps roots, flowers, and fruit start. Potassium builds overall strength and disease resistance.
Leafy crops (lettuce, kale) like more nitrogen. Fruiting crops (tomatoes, peppers) need balance — too much nitrogen gives big green plants with few fruits.
A soil test tells you what is actually missing, so you only add what helps. Log results in Soil & fertilizer.
lessons.tip: Compost is low in N-P-K but feeds soil life, which releases nutrients slowly over time.

quiz.q: Too much nitrogen on tomatoes usually causes…

sources.t: Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331 — Vegetable Planting Guide

lessons.title: Succession planting
body: Instead of sowing a whole row of lettuce at once, sow a short row every 2–3 weeks. You get a steady harvest instead of a glut followed by nothing.
Fast crops that suit this: radish, lettuce, bush beans, cilantro, and beets.
You can also follow one crop with another in the same bed: peas in spring, then bush beans in summer, then spinach in fall.
Use the crop library calendar to check the latest safe sowing date before your first fall frost.
lessons.tip: Keep a small tray of seedlings ready so you can fill gaps as soon as a crop comes out.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of succession planting?

sources.t: UF/IFAS SS480 — Soil pH and the Home Landscape or Garden
Univ. of Illinois Extension — When and How to Take a Soil Test

lessons.title: Soil pH in practice
body: pH measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, from 0 to 14; 7 is neutral.
Most vegetables grow best at 6.0–7.0, because that is where nutrients dissolve and stay available to roots.
Blueberries want acidic soil (4.5–5.5); garden lime raises pH and elemental sulfur lowers it. Both work slowly — re-test after a few months.
Change pH gradually and only based on a test, not a guess.
lessons.tip: Wood ash raises pH quickly — use it sparingly and never near blueberries or potatoes.

quiz.q: What pH range suits most vegetables?

sources.t: Open-Meteo weather data docs

lessons.title: Growing degree days
body: "Days to maturity" on a seed packet assumes average weather. Plants actually develop according to accumulated heat, measured in growing degree days (GDD).
For each day, GDD = ((daily max + daily min) / 2) − base temperature. Corn and beans use a base of 10 °C (50 °F); peas and spinach about 4 °C (40 °F). Days below the base add nothing.
That is why the same tomato ripens in 65 days in a hot summer and 90 in a cool one, and why insect pests emerge on predictable GDD totals each spring.
Tracking GDD from your local weather lets you time plantings and pest scouting more precisely than the calendar alone.
lessons.tip: Many extension services publish GDD targets for pests such as squash vine borer and codling moth.

quiz.q: With base 10 °C, a day with max 24 °C and min 12 °C adds how many GDD?

sources.t: Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331 — Vegetable Planting Guide

lessons.title: Using microclimates
body: Your zone and frost dates describe the region, but a garden contains microclimates that can differ by several degrees.

South-facing walls (north-facing in the Southern Hemisphere) store heat and release it at night — ideal for figs, peppers, and early starts. Cold air flows downhill and pools in low spots, creating frost pockets that freeze when the rest of the yard does not.
Paving, water bodies, and windbreaks moderate temperature; open, exposed sites lose heat fastest on clear, still nights.
Record winter-sun and frost observations per bed, then place tender perennials and early crops in the warmest spots.
lessons.tip: A cheap min/max thermometer in each bed for one season reveals your microclimates.

quiz.q: Where do frost pockets usually form?
options: In low spots where cold air settles

sources.t: Univ. of Missouri Extension G6203 — Common Diseases in the Home Garden

lessons.title: Designing a 4-year rotation
body: A classic rotation groups crops by family and nutrient demand: (1) legumes — peas, beans; (2) heavy-feeding leaf and fruit crops — brassicas, then nightshades or cucurbits; (3) roots — carrots, beets, onions; (4) a soil-building break with compost or cover crops.
Each bed moves one step per year, so a family returns only every 3–4 years, breaking cycles of soil-borne disease (clubroot, verticillium wilt, nematodes) and balancing nutrient use.
Real gardens rarely fit perfectly — prioritize keeping nightshades and brassicas out of the same bed for at least 3 years.
The rotation table on the Plantings page shows family history per bed; use it before you finalize next season's plan.
lessons.tip: Winter cover crops like cereal rye or crimson clover protect soil and add organic matter between rotations.

quiz.q: Which pair should you keep out of the same bed for at least 3 years?

sources.t: US EPA — Composting at Home
Univ. of Maryland Extension — How to Make Compost at Home

lessons.title: Turn scraps into compost
body: Compost is old plant stuff that has rotted. It turns into dark, crumbly food for your soil.
Tiny living things do the work. They eat fruit scraps, grass, and dry leaves.
You need two kinds of stuff. Greens are fruit and veggie scraps or fresh grass. Browns are dry leaves, twigs, and plain paper. Add two or three scoops of browns for each scoop of greens.
Keep meat, cheese, and oily food out. Keep the pile damp, but not dripping wet.
lessons.tip: If the pile smells bad, mix in more dry leaves and stir it.

quiz.q: Which one is a "brown" for compost?

lessons.title: Grow food in a pot
body: No yard? No problem! You can grow food in a pot on a porch or by a sunny window.
Pick a pot with a hole in the bottom. The hole lets extra water drain out.
Fill the whole pot with potting mix. It is light and fluffy, so roots grow easily. Do not put rocks in the bottom.
Lettuce, radishes, and herbs grow well in small pots. Tomatoes and peppers need a big pot, like a bucket.
Big plants in pots get thirsty. In hot weather, they may need water every day.
lessons.tip: Tomatoes need a pot that holds at least 5 gallons (about 19 liters).

quiz.q: Why does a pot need a hole in the bottom?
options: So extra water can drain out

lessons.title: Raised beds
body: A raised bed is a garden box. It sits up higher than the ground, and you fill it with good soil.
Soil in a raised bed warms up fast in spring. So you can often plant a little sooner.
Make the bed narrow. You should reach the middle from the side. Then you never step in it. Stepping in it packs the soil down hard.
Raised beds dry out faster than the ground. Check them for water often.
lessons.tip: Beds with low sides are easier for kids to reach.

quiz.q: Why should you not step inside a raised bed?
options: It makes plants grow too tall
It packs the soil down hard

sources.t: UMN Extension — Starting seeds indoors

lessons.title: Start seeds indoors
body: Some plants, like tomatoes and peppers, take a long time to grow. You can start their seeds inside while it is still cold outside.
Use small cups or trays with holes in the bottom. Fill them with seed-starting mix.
Seedlings need lots of light. A lamp right above them works better than a window. With too little light, the stems get tall, thin, and floppy.
Keep the mix damp, but not soggy. Read the seed packet to learn when to plant.
lessons.tip: Keep the lamp about 2 inches (5 cm) above the leaves. Raise it as the plants grow.

quiz.q: What makes seedlings tall, thin, and floppy?
options: Too many seeds in the packet

sources.t: Univ. of Maryland Extension — Hardening Off Vegetable Seedlings for the Home Garden
UMN Extension — Starting seeds indoors

lessons.title: Toughen up your seedlings
body: Plants grown inside are soft. Strong sun and wind outside can hurt them.
So we help them get tough, little by little. This is called hardening off. Start one to two weeks before you plant them in the garden.
On the first days, set them outside in a shady spot out of the wind. Bring them back in at night.
Each day, give them more time outside and more sun. Water them a little less, but do not let them droop.
lessons.tip: Keep seedlings inside on windy days or when it is colder than about 45 °F (7 °C).

quiz.q: How long does hardening off take?

sources.t: Clemson HGIC — Installing Drip Irrigation in Home Gardens
Iowa State Univ. Yard & Garden — Using Drip Irrigation in the Garden

lessons.title: Drip lines water the roots
body: A drip line is a thin hose with tiny holes. Water drips out slowly, right onto the soil by your plants.
Less water is lost. It does not blow away or run off. It soaks down to the roots, where plants drink.
The leaves stay dry. Dry leaves get sick less often.
Weeds between the rows get less water too, so fewer of them grow.
lessons.tip: Dirt can clog the tiny holes. A filter at the start of the line helps keep them clear.

quiz.q: Why is it good that drip lines keep leaves dry?
options: Dry leaves get sick less often

sources.t: Illinois Extension Good Growing — Flowers in the vegetable garden
UVM Extension — Encouraging Pollinators in Vegetable Gardens

lessons.title: Bees help make food
body: Bees, butterflies, and some flies and beetles are pollinators. They carry pollen from flower to flower.
Many foods need them. Squash, cucumbers, and melons cannot make fruit unless pollen gets moved.
Bumble bees can buzz to shake pollen loose. This helps tomatoes and peppers.
You can help pollinators. Plant lots of flowers, like zinnias and sunflowers, near your veggies. Try not to use bug sprays.
lessons.tip: Leave a little bare ground. Many wild bees make their nests in the soil.

quiz.q: Which plant needs pollinators to make its fruit?

sources.t: Cornell Cooperative Extension Warren County — Creating a Three Sisters Garden
UVM Extension — Encouraging Pollinators in Vegetable Gardens

lessons.title: Plants that help each other
body: Some plants are good neighbors. A famous team is the Three Sisters: corn, beans, and squash.
Native peoples of North America, such as the Iroquois, grew these three together.
Each one helps. Tall corn is a pole for the beans to climb. Beans help add nitrogen, a plant food, to the soil. Big, prickly squash leaves shade the ground. That helps stop weeds.
Flowers can be good neighbors too. They bring bees and bug-eating helpers to your garden.
lessons.tip: Plant the corn first. Plant the beans when the corn is about 6 inches (15 cm) tall.

quiz.q: In the Three Sisters, how does the corn help the beans?
options: It gives them a pole to climb

sources.t: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Garden Tools
Illinois Extension — Garden Tool Maintenance
NDSU Extension — Gardening with Children
Rutgers Cooperative Extension FS003 — Gardening Activities for Youth

lessons.title: Use tools safely
body: Garden tools help you dig, rake, and cut. Some are sharp, so be careful.
Wear gloves to keep your hands safe. Wear long pants and closed shoes, not sandals.
Kids should use kid-size tools. Always ask a grown-up before you use anything sharp.
When you are done, brush off the dirt. Put tools away in a dry place. This stops rust. It also keeps plant germs from spreading.
lessons.tip: Never use garden sprays or plant food without a grown-up.

quiz.q: What should you do with tools when you finish?
options: Put them in a bucket of water
Clean them and put them away dry

sources.t: UMN Extension — Saving vegetable seeds

lessons.title: Save your own seeds
body: You can save seeds from your garden and plant them next year!
Beans, peas, tomatoes, and peppers are easy ones to start with.
Look for plants called open-pollinated or heirloom. Seeds from hybrid plants may grow into plants that are not like the parent.
For beans and peas, let the pods dry on the plant. Wait until they turn brown and the seeds rattle. Then dry them more inside.
Keep seeds in a closed jar in a cool, dry place.
lessons.tip: Write the plant name and the date on your seed jar. Use saved seeds within a year.

quiz.q: When are bean seeds ready to save?
options: When the pods are small and green
When the pods are dry and the seeds rattle

sources.t: SDSU Extension — Fall Vegetable Garden Cleanup
Iowa State Univ. Yard & Garden — How can I minimize plant disease problems next year?
UVM Extension — Encouraging Pollinators in Vegetable Gardens
Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331 — Vegetable Planting Guide and Recommended Planting Dates

lessons.title: Fall garden cleanup
body: When the garden is done for the year, it is time to tidy up. First, pick any veggies that are left.
Pull out sick plants, roots and all. Put them in the trash, not the compost. Germs can hide in old plants all winter.
Healthy old plants are good for the soil. Chop them up and add them to your compost.
Dry leaves are good, too. Spread them on empty beds to help the soil.
In places with mild winters, fall can be a time to plant, not just clean up!
lessons.tip: Leave some hollow plant stems standing in one corner. Some bees spend the winter inside them.

quiz.q: Where should sick plants go?

sources.t: Nebraska Extension NebGuide G1953 — Understanding the Seed Packet
UMaine Cooperative Extension — When does "days to maturity" start?

lessons.title: Read a seed packet
body: A seed packet is like a tiny guide. Read the back before you plant.
Planting depth tells how deep to put the seed. Spacing tells how far apart to plant.
Light tells how much sun the plant needs. Full sun means six hours or more each day.
When to sow often says how many weeks before or after your last frost.
Days to maturity tells about how long until you can pick. It is only a guess. Weather can make it faster or slower.
lessons.tip: Keep leftover seeds in a closed jar in the fridge so they stay fresh.

quiz.q: What does "days to maturity" tell you?
options: About how long until you can pick

sources.t: Rutgers Cooperative Extension FS003 — Gardening Activities for Youth
NDSU Extension — Gardening with Children

lessons.title: Garden jobs for kids
body: Everyone can help in the garden! There is a job for every age.
Little kids can water plants and dig with small tools. They can fill seed trays with potting soil. A grown-up should always watch them.
Bigger kids can start seeds, rake leaves, and pick veggies. They can help make a compost pile, too.
Older kids can help plan the garden. They can pick what to grow.
Try a bean teepee! Tie poles together and plant beans around them. The beans climb up and make a green hideout.
lessons.tip: Give each kid one plant or a small patch that is all theirs to care for.

quiz.q: Who should always be with little kids in the garden?

sources.t: Illinois Extension — Cover Crops in the Home Garden
Iowa State Univ. Yard & Garden — How to Terminate Cover Crops in the Vegetable Garden

lessons.title: Cover crops feed the soil
body: A cover crop is a plant you grow to help the soil, not to eat.
You plant it in an empty bed. Many people plant one in late summer or fall, after the harvest.
Its roots help loosen hard soil. It helps keep weeds down. Some cover crops, like clover, add nitrogen. When the plants break down, they feed the soil.
In cold places, oats are an easy pick. Winter kills them, so they turn into mulch.
Stop the cover crop two to three weeks before you plant your veggies.
lessons.tip: Cut your cover crop down before it makes seeds. If it drops seeds, it can turn into a weed.

quiz.q: What is a cover crop for?

sources.t: USDA ARS — 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map
NOAA Climate.gov — Average date of last spring freeze
Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331 — Vegetable Planting Guide and Recommended Planting Dates
RHS — Hardiness ratings

lessons.title: Frost dates vs. hardiness zones
body: Two numbers help you plan a garden. They sound alike, but they mean different things.

The first is your hardiness zone. In the US, the USDA zone map is based on how cold your winters get on average. It tells you which perennials can live through your winter. Perennials are plants that come back year after year. Other countries have their own systems. In the UK, the RHS gives plants a rating from H1a to H7. It shows the lowest cold each plant can take.

The second is your frost dates. The last spring frost is the average date of the last cold night in spring. The first fall frost is the average date of the first cold night in fall. The time between them is your growing season. Seed packs count weeks from these dates, so they guide most vegetable planting.

An average date is not a promise. Right after the average last frost, the odds of no more frost are only a bit better than half. So keep a cover close by for tender plants like tomatoes and peppers for a few weeks.

Your zone alone will not tell you your frost dates. For example, Virginia Extension lists the average last spring frost as about April 15 to 25 in zone 7a. In zone 6a, it is about May 5 to 15. Look up the frost dates for your own town, not just your zone.
lessons.tip: Look up your own last and first frost dates, then count your planting weeks from them.

quiz.q: What is a USDA hardiness zone based on?

sources.t: UC Statewide IPM Program — What is Integrated Pest Management?
Wisconsin Horticulture — Strategies for Identifying and Managing Insect Pests

lessons.title: Pest control the IPM way
body: IPM stands for integrated pest management. It is a smart way to handle bugs. You stop problems before they start. You use bug sprays only when you really need them.
First, look at your plants often. Find out just what the bug or problem is. Many bugs do no harm. Some even help you. Knowing how a pest grows tells you the best time to act.
Next, ask if the harm matters. A few holes in leaves are often fine.

If you need to act, use more than one way. Keep plants healthy and pick strong kinds. Water the right way. Pick bugs off by hand. Use row covers or mulch. Let good bugs, like lady beetles, eat the pests. Flowers bring good bugs in. Sprays come last.
lessons.tip: Even organic sprays can hurt good bugs. If a spray is needed, an adult should use it, and only on the plants that need it.

quiz.q: In IPM, what should you do before choosing a control?
options: Spray the whole garden to be safe
Look closely and find out what the pest is

sources.t: Wisconsin Horticulture — Trellising, Staking and Caging

lessons.title: Grow up: trellises, stakes, and cages
body: Some plants grow long vines. You can help them climb up instead of out. This saves space on the ground.
Growing up has other good points. Air moves through the leaves, so plants get sick less. Fruit stays clean, off the dirt. There is less weeding. And it is easy to pick at arm height.
Good plants to grow up are pole beans, peas, tomatoes, cucumbers, melons, squash, and gourds.
Tomatoes cannot hold on by themselves. Put them in a cage. Or tie them to a stake. Peas and cucumbers grow thin curly arms called tendrils. Tendrils grab the trellis on their own.
Vines get stronger as fruit grows. But big fruit, like melons, may need a sling made of cloth or mesh.
lessons.tip: Put cages and stakes in on planting day. Then you will not hurt roots and stems later.

quiz.q: Which crop needs tying or a cage because it can't grab a trellis on its own?

sources.t: Utah State Univ. Extension — Row Covers
Illinois Extension — Cold Frames Extend the Garden Season
Univ. of Maryland Extension — Hardening Off Vegetable Seedlings for the Home Garden

lessons.title: Stretch the season: row covers and cold frames
body: You can grow food earlier in spring and later in fall. Two simple tools help: row covers and cold frames.
A row cover is a thin, light cloth. You lay it over plants or hold it up on wire hoops. Thick covers keep plants safe from frost. Thin covers are mostly used to keep bugs out.

Covers keep bees out too. Squash, cucumbers, pumpkins, and melons need bees to make fruit. So take the cover off these plants once they start to bloom. Weeds grow fast under covers, so lift the cover now and then to pull them.

A cold frame is a low box with a clear lid, like a tiny greenhouse. It traps the sun's warmth and blocks the wind. It can add one to three months to your season. Grow lettuce and radishes in it early or late in the year. You can also use it to toughen up young plants before they go in the garden.
Both can get too hot on sunny days. Under a row cover, it can be 5 to 15 °F (3 to 8 °C) warmer than outside. So open the covers and prop up the cold frame lid when it is warm.
lessons.tip: Try lettuce or radishes in a cold frame for an early spring salad.

quiz.q: When should you take row covers off squash and cucumbers?
options: When the plants start to flower
As soon as you plant them

sources.t: UMN Extension — Watering the vegetable garden
Iowa State Univ. Yard & Garden — Watering the Home Vegetable Garden

lessons.title: Watering by soil type
body: Most vegetable gardens need about 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water each week. That counts rain and the water you add. Hot, dry, windy days mean plants need more.

Your soil type helps set the plan. Sandy soil does not hold much water. You may need to water about two times a week. Clay soil, or soil with lots of compost, holds more water. Once a week is often enough. Mulch helps any soil stay moist longer.
Water slowly and deeply. Let the water soak 6 to 12 inches (15 to 30 cm) down. That is where most vegetable roots grow. A deep soak now and then is better than a little splash every day.

Check the soil before you water. Pull back the mulch and dig a small hole with a trowel. If the soil is dry 2 inches (5 cm) down, it is time to water. A rain gauge shows how much water fell. An empty tuna can under the sprinkler works too.
lessons.tip: Water in the morning so the leaves can dry fast.

quiz.q: Which soil usually needs watering most often?

sources.t: Colorado State Univ. Extension — The Living Soil
Clemson HGIC — Why Does Soil Health Matter? Starting with Soil Organisms

lessons.title: The soil food web
body: Soil is full of life. One cup of wild soil that no one has dug may hold up to 200 billion bacteria. It may also hold 20 million tiny protozoa, 100,000 nematodes, and 50,000 small bugs. Its fungus threads could stretch about 100,000 meters. Colorado State Extension says we have named only about 1% of soil life.

These living things eat dead leaves and roots. They also eat each other. As they eat, they let go of plant food in a form roots can drink up. This is called mineralization. They also glue soil into soft crumbs, so air and water can move.

Some team up with plants. Rhizobia are bacteria that live in little bumps on bean and pea roots. They pull nitrogen from the air and give it to the plant. Mycorrhizal fungi join roots and act like extra roots. They help the plant reach more water and food.

Most soil life works best when soil is warm and damp. In cold soil it slows down. So food that microbes must break down works slowly in cold spring soil. To feed soil life, add compost and use mulch. Do not dig more than you need to, because digging breaks fungus threads and soil crumbs. Do not let soil stay soggy. Skip bug sprays you do not need.
lessons.tip: Use mulch, not digging, to stop weeds. It keeps the fungus threads safe and feeds soil life.

quiz.q: Why might an organic fertilizer act slowly in cold spring soil?
options: It freezes into a solid block
Soil organisms that release its nutrients are less active in cool soil
Roots cannot take up any nutrients until summer

sources.t: NMSU Extension Guide H-262 — Vegetable Seed Saving for Home Gardeners
UC Master Gardeners of Placer County — Saving Seeds chart
Univ. of Maryland Extension — Seed Saving 101: Vegetables

lessons.title: Seed saving: isolation and purity
body: Saved seed grows a plant like its parent only if the flower got pollen from the same kind of plant. Beans, peas, lettuce, and tomatoes mostly pollinate themselves. They rarely mix. Squash, cucumbers, corn, spinach, and the cabbage family get pollen from bugs or wind. They mix easily.

Plants only mix inside the same species. A species is one group of plants that can breed. Zucchini and yellow crookneck squash are both Cucurbita pepo, so they can mix. But pepo, maxima, and moschata squash mostly do not mix with each other.

Isolation distance is how far apart two kinds of the same species should grow. One UC Master Gardener chart gives these. Lettuce and peas: about 50 ft (15 m). Tomatoes: 25 to 100 ft (8 to 30 m). Peppers: 500 ft (150 m). Cucumbers, squash, carrots, onions, and radishes: 1,500 ft (460 m). Beets, chard, cabbage family, melons, and spinach: half a mile (800 m). Sources do not all agree. NMSU says two miles for corn.

No room? Plant at different times so the kinds bloom at different times. Or cover flowers with a bag or cage and move the pollen by hand. Save seed from many plants, not just one. That keeps more variety in the seed. Only save seed from open-pollinated plants. Seed from hybrid plants will not grow true.
lessons.tip: If you only have room for one kind of a crop that mixes, grow just that one kind the year you save its seed.

quiz.q: Zucchini and yellow crookneck squash grow a block apart. Will seed saved from the zucchini likely be pure?
options: Yes, because they are different vegetables
No, both are Cucurbita pepo and bees can cross them

sources.t: UMN Extension — Managing plant diseases in the home garden
UGA Extension C862 — Disease Management in the Home Vegetable Garden

lessons.title: Keep plants from getting sick
body: Plants can get sick too. Tiny germs called fungi and bacteria can cause spots, rot, and wilting leaves.
These germs love wet leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves. Water early in the day so plants dry fast in the sun. Give plants room so air can move around them.
Look at your plants once a week. If you see a leaf with spots, ask an adult to help pinch it off and take it out of the garden. Never take off more than one third of a plant's leaves.
Stay out of the garden when the leaves are wet. Germs can ride on your hands to the next plant.
lessons.tip: When you buy seeds or plants, look for ones that say they resist disease.

quiz.q: When is the best time to water so leaves dry fast?
options: Any time, on top of the leaves

sources.t: MU Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

lessons.title: Grow your own herbs
body: Herbs are plants we use to give food more flavor. Basil, chives, dill, and mint are all herbs.
Most herbs love the sun. Give them 6 to 8 hours of sunlight each day. Sun helps them make the oils that give them their smell and taste.
Most herbs do not like wet feet. Plant them where water drains away, or in a raised bed. Mint is one herb that likes damper soil.
Herbs do not need rich soil. Too much fertilizer makes lots of leaves with less flavor.
lessons.tip: Plant dill and fennel seeds right where they will grow. They do not like to be moved.

quiz.q: How much sun do most herbs want each day?

sources.t: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Radishes

lessons.title: Radishes grow fast
body: Want to see food grow fast? Try radishes! The seeds sprout quickly, and many radishes are ready to pick in about 20 to 30 days.
Plant the tiny seeds no more than a quarter inch deep, right where they will grow. Radishes do not like to be moved.
Radishes like cool weather. Hot weather can make them taste sharp and bitter. Plant them when the weather is cool where you live. In warm places like Florida, that means fall and winter.
Pick them while they are young. If you wait too long, they get tough. Young radish leaves are good to eat too!
lessons.tip: Plant a few more seeds every couple of weeks so you keep picking radishes all season.

quiz.q: What happens if radishes stay in the ground too long?

sources.t: Oregon State Extension EM 9308 — How to use compost in gardens and landscapes
WSU Extension — Organic soil amendments in yards and gardens: How much is enough?
CSU Extension — Vegetable Gardens: Soil Management and Fertilization

lessons.title: Soil amendments: how much compost to add
body: An amendment is stuff you mix into soil. It helps soil hold water, drain, and feed roots. Good ones are compost, compost made with manure, chopped leaves, straw, coconut coir, and peat moss. Mulch sits on top of soil. An amendment gets mixed in.

For a new veggie bed, Oregon State Extension says to spread 3 to 4 inches of compost. Mix it into the top 8 to 12 inches. Washington State says 1 to 3 inches, mixed 6 to 8 inches deep. Use the most for pale soil that has little organic matter.
Old beds need much less. Add about 1/4 to 1 inch a year. WSU says about 1/2 inch. To plan, 3 cubic yards of compost covers about 1,000 square feet, 1 inch deep.

More is not always better. Compost made with manure or biosolids can be salty. So Colorado State says to use less of it, unless a test shows the salt is low. If a soil test shows lots of phosphorus, use less compost or skip it. Let a soil test guide lime and fertilizer. Keep them away from kids.
lessons.tip: One cubic yard of compost covers about 325 square feet, 1 inch deep. That helps when you buy compost by the truckload.

quiz.q: Your bed has been amended for several years. About how much compost should you add this year?
options: 3 to 4 inches, the same as a new bed

sources.t: SDSU Extension P-00379 — Square-Foot Garden Sample Planting Layout
UW–Madison Extension Taylor County — Square Foot Gardening
UF/IFAS Extension Leon County — Square Foot Vegetable Planting Guide for Northwest Florida

lessons.title: Square-foot gardening
body: Square-foot gardening splits a bed into a grid of squares. Each square is 1 foot on each side. You plant one crop in each square. A 4 by 4 foot frame, about 6 to 8 inches deep, gives 16 squares. Keep beds 4 feet wide or less. If you can reach from only one side, keep them 2 feet wide. That way you never step on the soil.

Here is how to find plants per square. Divide 12 by the spacing on the seed packet. Then times the answer by itself. For 3 inch spacing, 12 divided by 3 is 4, and 4 times 4 is 16 plants. For 4 inch spacing you get 9. For 6 inches you get 4. For 12 inches you get 1.

SDSU Extension gives examples. Put 16 in a square for radishes, carrots, green onions, and beets. Put 9 for bush beans, spinach, and garlic. Put 4 for lettuce, chard, and basil. Put 1 for broccoli, cabbage, peppers, eggplant, and parsley. Big plants like summer squash may need 4 squares for one plant.
Spacing depends on the kind of plant. If plants get crowded, change it next year. When you pick a square, add a bit of compost. Then plant a different crop there.
lessons.tip: Mark the grid with string, thin wood strips, or old blinds. Leave it in place all season.

quiz.q: A seed packet says to space plants 6 inches apart. How many go in one square foot?

sources.t: Illinois Extension — Vermicomposting

lessons.title: Worms that make compost
body: A worm bin is a box where worms turn food scraps into rich compost. People call this worm composting.
Use red wigglers, not worms from your yard. Red wigglers live near the top of the ground and eat a lot. In one day, they can eat more than half of what they weigh!
Fill the bin with torn newspaper. Make it damp, like a sponge you squeezed out. Add a pinch of sand or crushed eggshell. Worms have no teeth, so this grit helps them mash food.
Feed them raw fruit and veggie scraps, cut small. Keep out meat, cheese, and oily or salty food. Keep the bin out of the sun, between 55 and 80°F.
lessons.tip: Bury new scraps under the damp paper so the bin won't smell.

quiz.q: Which food should stay out of a worm bin?

sources.t: UW–Madison Extension, Wisconsin Horticulture — Rain Barrels
U.S. EPA — Soak Up the Rain: Rain Barrels

lessons.title: Catch rain in a barrel
body: A rain barrel sits under a downspout. It catches the rain that runs off a roof. You can use that free water on flowers, bushes, and grass.
A roof sheds a lot of water. One inch of rain on a 1,000 square foot roof makes about 600 gallons!
Roof water can pick up germs and chemicals. Experts say not to use it on food plants, and never drink it.
Put a fine screen on top so mosquitoes can't get in to lay eggs. Use the water within a week. Where winters freeze, drain the barrel in fall so it won't crack.
lessons.tip: A full barrel is very heavy and can tip. Never climb on it. Ask an adult to set it on a strong, flat base.

quiz.q: What should a rain barrel have on top?

sources.t: Illinois Extension, ILRiverHort — Garden Journal: A helpful gardening tool

lessons.title: Keep a garden journal
body: A garden journal is a book about your garden. It helps you remember what went well and what did not.
It can be a notebook, a binder, or an app on a phone. Pick the one that is easy for you to use.
Write the date and the weather. Write when you plant, when flowers open, and when you pick food. Draw a map of where each plant grows. Next year, you can use it to move crops to new spots.
Tape in seed packets and plant tags. Add drawings or photos of your best plants. You don't have to write every day. Just pick a time and stick to it.
lessons.tip: Write in your journal right after you check the garden, while you still remember what you saw.

quiz.q: Why draw a map of your garden?
options: To plan where crops go next year

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing garlic in home gardens

lessons.title: Plant garlic in the fall
body: Garlic is a cousin of onions and chives. To grow it, you plant one clove. Each clove grows into a whole new bulb!
Where winters are cold, plant garlic in fall, a week or two after the first hard frost. Push each clove in with the pointy end up. Set it 2 to 3 inches deep and 6 inches apart.
Cover the bed with 3 to 4 inches of straw or leaves. This keeps weeds down. Green shoots pop up in spring.
Dig garlic in summer. It is ready when the low leaves turn brown but about half of the top leaves are still green. Dry it in a warm, airy spot for 3 to 4 weeks.
lessons.tip: Buy garlic for planting from a seed seller. Garlic from the store may not grow well where you live.

quiz.q: Which way should a garlic clove point when you plant it?

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — Growing Sunflowers and Their Varieties
NC State Extension, Grow For It — Planting Sunflowers

lessons.title: Grow sunflowers
body: Sunflowers love the sun. Plant them in a spot that gets full sun.
In spring, push the seeds 1 to 2 inches into the soil. They sprout in 1 to 2 weeks. Young sunflowers don't like to be moved, so plant seeds right where they will grow.
Some kinds grow taller than 8 feet and may need a stake to hold them up. Small kinds stay 3 feet or shorter and fit in a pot.
Once they are big, sunflowers can live through dry spells. But give them water while the flowers and seeds form. Watch out for birds. They love the seeds too!
lessons.tip: Measure your sunflower each week and write it down. See how fast it grows!

quiz.q: How much sun do sunflowers need?

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — How to Protect Plants from Frost and Freeze
Colorado State University Extension — Frost Protection and Extending the Growing Season

lessons.title: Tuck plants in on a frosty night
body: Some plants, like tomatoes and peppers, get hurt by frost. When the weather report says a cold night is coming, you can help them.
Plants in small pots are easy. Carry them inside to a garage or a warm room for the night.

For plants in the ground, cover them in the evening. An old sheet, a blanket, or garden cloth works. Prop it up with sticks or buckets so it does not touch the leaves. The cover holds in warm air from the soil.
Take the cover off the next day when the air warms up. On a very cold night, a cover may not be enough.
lessons.tip: Keep the cover dry. A wet blanket can make the plants under it colder.

quiz.q: When should you take the frost cover off?
options: The next day, once it warms up

sources.t: University of Illinois Extension — Organic Mulches
Iowa State University Extension — Using Mulch in the Garden

lessons.title: Fallen leaves make free mulch
body: In the fall, trees drop lots of leaves. Do not throw them away! They can be a free blanket for your garden.
Chop the leaves into small bits first. An adult can run a lawn mower over them. Small bits do not blow away as much, and they do not pack into a thick mat.
Spread the bits 2 to 4 inches deep on your garden. They help stop weeds and keep the soil wet. As they rot, they feed the soil too.
lessons.tip: Pile up extra chopped leaves. In a year or two, they turn into dark, crumbly leaf mold.

quiz.q: Why chop leaves before using them as mulch?
options: So bugs can not find them
So they stay put and rot faster

sources.t: RHS — How to grow lettuces

lessons.title: Grow lettuce for salads
body: Lettuce is quick and easy to grow. It fits in a garden bed or even a pot.
Plant the tiny seeds about half an inch deep. When they come up, pull out a few so the rest have room. You can eat the ones you pull!
Leaf lettuce can be ready about a month after you plant it. Cut some leaves, and more will grow back.
Lettuce likes cool weather. Hot, dry days can make it flower and taste bitter. Keep the soil wet, and give it some shade in summer. Plant a few more seeds every two weeks so you always have salad.
lessons.tip: Watch out for slugs and snails. They love lettuce too!

quiz.q: What can make lettuce taste bitter?

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Tomato hornworms
University of Minnesota Extension — Colorado potato beetles

lessons.title: Pick big bugs off by hand
body: Some garden pests are big and easy to see. You can stop them without any spray. Just pick them off!
Tomato hornworms are huge green caterpillars with a horn on the tail. They eat tomato leaves fast. Look for their dark poop on the leaves below.
Colorado potato beetles have yellow and black stripes. Look under potato leaves for their orange eggs, and rub them off.
Wear gloves. Drop the bugs into a cup of soapy water. Check your plants two times a week in summer.
See a hornworm with white bumps like rice? Leave it! Tiny helper wasps are growing inside.
lessons.tip: Not sure what a bug is? Ask an adult to help you look it up before you pick it.

quiz.q: A hornworm has white bumps like rice on it. What should you do?

sources.t: RHS — Nutrient deficiencies
University of Delaware Cooperative Extension — Identifying Nutrient Deficiencies in Ornamental Plants
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Guide to Symptoms of Plant Nutrient Deficiencies

lessons.title: Reading nutrient deficiencies in leaves
body: Pale, yellow, or purple leaves may mean a plant is short on a nutrient. A nutrient is plant food. But other things look the same. Too little water, too much water, cold, low light, and weak roots can all do it. Check those first.

Look at where the trouble starts. That is the best clue. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium can move in the plant. When they run low, the plant takes them from old leaves to feed new ones. So old, low leaves show the problem first. Calcium, iron, sulfur, boron, and most tiny nutrients barely move. So new leaves show those problems first.

Here are some common signs. Low nitrogen makes a small plant that is pale yellow all over, starting on old leaves. Low magnesium turns old leaves yellow between the veins, but the veins stay green. Low iron looks the same, but on the newest leaves. It is most likely when soil has a high pH, or too much lime.

Fix the cause, not just the sign. Lots of potassium feed, like tomato food, can block magnesium. High pH can lock up iron. Plants in pots run out of food faster than plants in the ground. Test the soil before you add anything. Use fertilizer just as the label says, and keep it away from kids.
lessons.tip: Before you buy a fix, check if the trouble began on the oldest or the newest leaves. That one clue rules out a lot.

quiz.q: Yellowing between the veins of the newest leaves, with the veins still green, most likely points to a shortage of what?

sources.t: University of Illinois Extension — Home Hydroponics handouts
University of Missouri Extension — Controlled Environment Agriculture: Hydroponic Farming (G6986)
UNH Extension — Hydroponics at Home

lessons.title: Plants that grow in water
body: Hydroponics means growing plants with no soil. The roots sit in water instead.
Soil is where plants get their food. In hydroponics, we mix plant food into the water. The roots drink it up.
Some setups use a pump to move the water. A simple kind uses a wick, like a thick string, to pull water up to the roots.
Lettuce, herbs, and strawberries grow well this way. Ask an adult to mix the plant food. Keep it away from little kids.
lessons.tip: Keep light off the water. Light helps green slime called algae grow.

quiz.q: In hydroponics, what do the roots grow in instead of soil?
options: Air with no water at all

sources.t: NMSU Extension — Important Water Quality Parameters in Aquaponics Systems (CR-680)
SRAC Publication 454 — Aquaponics: Integrating Fish and Plant Culture (University of Kentucky)

lessons.title: Fish and plants help each other
body: Aquaponics is a garden with fish in it. The fish live in a tank. The plants grow in water next to it.
Fish make waste. Tiny helpers called bacteria change that waste into plant food.
The plants eat the food. That cleans the water, so it can flow back to the fish.
Herbs like basil and greens like lettuce grow well this way. A pump moves the water. Water and power can be a bad mix, so an adult should set it up.
lessons.tip: Tap water from the city has chlorine in it. An adult must take it out before fish go in.

quiz.q: What turns fish waste into plant food?
