sources.t: FAO — Small-scale aquaponic food production (Fisheries Technical Paper 589), duckweed as fish feed
FAO AGRIS — Nutritive value of duckweed (Lemna) for Nile tilapia
Texas A&M AgriLife EHT-148 — Aquaponics: Fish Species Selection

lessons.title: Grow duckweed for fish food
body: Duckweed is a tiny plant that floats on water. Each one is about the size of a lentil. It grows very fast. In good weather it can double in a day or two.
Fish like it. Tilapia and carp eat it well. Koi and goldfish are kinds of carp, and they nibble it too.
Grow it in its own tub, not in the fish tank. Fish would eat it all. Loose bits can also clog the pump and the filter.

Give the tub sun or part shade. Let a slow trickle of water from the plant beds run through it on the way back to the fish. That water has plant food in it, so you do not need to add any. You do not need an air pump.
The duckweed also soaks up food the plants missed. So the water going back to the fish is cleaner.
lessons.tip: Start with a small scoop from a store or a friend. Never take it from a lake or a river. It can carry germs to your fish.

quiz.q: Where should you grow duckweed?

sources.t: FAO — Small-scale aquaponic food production (Fisheries Technical Paper 589), duckweed as fish feed
FAO AGRIS — Nutritive value of duckweed (Lemna) for Nile tilapia
Texas A&M AgriLife EHT-148 — Aquaponics: Fish Species Selection
UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants — Dotted duckweed
Texas A&M AquaPlant — Dotted duckweed

lessons.title: Pick and feed duckweed
body: When duckweed covers the top of the tub, it is time to pick. Skim off about a third to half with a net. The rest grows back.
Dry duckweed is about 30 parts protein out of 100. Protein helps fish grow. But fresh duckweed is mostly water.
Use it as a treat, not the whole meal. FAO says fresh duckweed can be up to about 1 out of 10 parts of what fish eat each day. Keep giving them fish food too. Take out what they leave.
Put extra duckweed in bags and freeze it for later.

Do not let it get out. It can cover a pond, and the fish below can run out of air. Some places ban some kinds of duckweed, so check your local rules. Never dump it in a pond, a stream or a drain. Seal extra in a bag and put it in the trash.
Cold weather slows it down. Before frost, keep a small tub inside by a bright window or under a grow light. Then you can start again when it warms up.
lessons.tip: Rinse your net in the duckweed tub, not in a pond, so no bits ride along.

quiz.q: How much duckweed should you skim off at one time?

sources.t: University of Missouri Extension — Controlled Environment Agriculture: Hydroponic Farming (G6986)
UF/IFAS Extension Lee County — Hydroponic Production Methods, Part 1

lessons.title: Roots that hang in the air
body: Aeroponics is one more way to grow plants with no soil. The roots hang in the air inside a box or tube.
A pump sprays a fine mist of water and plant food onto the roots. The mist keeps them wet.
This way uses less water than other soil-free gardens. It can stack up tall, so it fits in small spaces.
But if the pump stops, the roots dry out fast and the plants wilt. Lettuce and herbs grow well this way. An adult should handle the pump and the plant food.
lessons.tip: Check every day that the mister is still spraying.

quiz.q: What happens if an aeroponics pump stops?
options: The roots dry out and the plants wilt

sources.t: Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC — Hobby Greenhouses
CSU Extension PlantTalk Colorado — Hobby Greenhouses: Heating & Cooling

lessons.title: What a greenhouse does
body: A greenhouse is a room with clear walls and a clear roof. Sun comes in and warms the air.
On a sunny winter day, it can be warm inside even when it is cold outside. That helps plants grow longer.
But it can get too hot, too. Vents up high let hot air out. Vents down low let cool air in. Fans help mix the air.
In cold places, a greenhouse may need a heater at night. An adult should set up any heater, since some give off bad gas.
lessons.tip: Hang a thermometer at plant height so you know how warm your plants really are.

quiz.q: Why does a greenhouse have vents?

sources.t: UNH Extension — Hydroponics at Home

lessons.title: Hydroponic nutrient solution: pH and EC
body: In hydroponics there is no soil to hold plant food. So the water has to carry all of it. Plants need 13 nutrients, like nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and calcium. A fertilizer made for hydroponics, mixed in water, gives them all. For leafy greens, pick a veggie or grow mix, not a bloom mix.

Start with water that is safe to drink. Well water and city water both work. pH tells how sour or not the water is. It changes how well roots take up tiny nutrients. Big farms fine-tune it. But UNH Extension says a pH from 5.5 to 7.0 is fine for a home system.

EC means electrical conductivity. It is a fast way to guess how much fertilizer is in the water. Once you have grown for a while, an EC meter can guide you. If the number is too high, add plain water. If it is too low, add more plant food.
Do not pour old water down the drain. Its nitrogen and phosphorus feed algae in streams and lakes. Use it on garden beds or the lawn instead.
lessons.tip: Have an adult mix strong fertilizer and any pH up or pH down. They should wear gloves and keep it away from kids.

quiz.q: Your EC reading is higher than you want. What's the simple fix?

sources.t: NMSU Extension — Important Water Quality Parameters in Aquaponics Systems (CR-680)

lessons.title: Aquaponics: the nitrogen cycle and cycling a new system
body: Fish give off ammonia. Most of it comes out of their gills. Ammonia is a poison to fish. In aquaponics, good bacteria clean it up in two steps. First, one kind, Nitrosomonas, turns ammonia into nitrite. Nitrite is a poison too. Next, a second kind, Nitrobacter, turns nitrite into nitrate. Nitrate is mostly safe for fish. Plants use it as food.
Both steps use up oxygen. They also make the water more sour, so the pH slowly drops. NMSU Extension says a pH of 6.8 to 7.0 is best for fish, plants, and bacteria all at once.

A new system must be cycled. That means you wait while the bacteria grow. Test ammonia and nitrite each day at the start. Wait until nitrate shows up. Wait until ammonia and nitrite are both 0.5 ppm or less. Then the system is cycled. After that, a test once a week is most often enough.
If ammonia goes up, feed less. Add more air bubbles, or add fresh water. City water has chlorine or chloramine in it. Take those out before the water goes in.
lessons.tip: Write down every test number. Then you can see a problem coming before it gets bad.

quiz.q: Which form of nitrogen do the plants use as fertilizer?

sources.t: NMSU Extension — Important Water Quality Parameters in Aquaponics Systems (CR-680)
Kentucky State University — Aquaponics Handbook (2021)
Utah Division of Wildlife Resources — Aquaponics: Raising your own fish for food

lessons.title: Picking fish for aquaponics
body: Each kind of fish likes water at a certain heat. Goldfish, bass, catfish, and tilapia are warm-water fish. They like water from 65 to 85°F. Bluegill are warm-water fish too. Trout are cold-water fish. They like 55 to 65°F. Pick fish that fit the water you can keep.
Tilapia are the fish used most. They can take crowding and water that is not perfect. They grow best at 81 to 85°F. Below about 75°F they grow slowly and get sick more easily.

Koi are tough, and you can buy them all year. Koi are a bright kind of carp. They are a good pick if the fish are just there to feed the plants. Catfish have sharp barbs on their heads, so they can hurt each other at feeding time. Trout need very clean water with lots of air in it.

Fish rules are not the same in every state. Some fish need a permit, and some are not allowed at all. In Utah, for example, home aquaponics fish may never be let go into the wild. Ask an adult to check your state's wildlife rules before you buy fish.
lessons.tip: Never dump tank fish into a pond or creek. Ask your state wildlife office what to do with extra fish.

quiz.q: Which fish likes cold water?

sources.t: University of Missouri Extension — Controlled Environment Agriculture: Hydroponic Farming (G6986)
UF/IFAS Extension Lee County — Hydroponic Production Methods, Part 1
UMass Amherst Extension — Mist and Fog Equipment for Propagation
Auburn University — Design Guidelines for Aeroponic Plant Growth Systems (thesis)

lessons.title: Aeroponics: how the mist feeds roots
body: In aeroponics, roots hang in a dark, closed box. Sprayers mist them with water and plant food. A timer turns the mist on and off. Between sprays, the roots get lots of air. That helps the plants take in food and grow fast.
Special pumps push the water through very small holes in the sprayers. That makes a fine mist, almost like fog. Very fine drops float in the air and stick to the roots. Big drops fall down too fast.

Small holes clog easily. Hard water can leave a crust inside pipes and sprayers. Use filtered water or rain water. Put a fine screen filter in the line, and clean it often. Clean the root box between crops.
Here is the big risk. If the pump stops or a sprayer clogs, the roots dry out. The plants wilt right away. So check the sprayers and the timer often.
lessons.tip: Pumps and timers use electricity near water. Have an adult set them up and check them.

quiz.q: What happens if the pump stops in aeroponics?

sources.t: UGA Extension — Hobby Greenhouses (B910)
UMass Amherst Extension — Ventilation for Greenhouses
UMass Amherst Extension — Problems With Using Unvented Greenhouse Heaters
Farm Energy (extension.org) — Greenhouse Unit Heaters: Types, Placement, and Efficiency (A3907-02)

lessons.title: Greenhouse air: letting heat out and keeping it in
body: A greenhouse traps the sun's heat. Even on a cold, sunny day, it can get hot enough to hurt or kill plants. So every greenhouse needs a way to let hot air out.

Hot air rises. Vents in the roof let it out. Cool air comes in low, through side vents. Wind does most of this work. On still, hot days, a fan helps. In summer, the fan should push out all the air in the greenhouse about once a minute.
A thermostat can run the fans for you. It turns them on when it gets hot and off when it cools down. Then no one has to open and shut vents all day.

On cold nights, a heater keeps plants warm. Some gas and kerosene heaters have no pipe to the outside. Their fumes stay inside. The fumes can hold carbon monoxide, which is a danger to people. They can hold gases that hurt plants too. A heater with a pipe that vents outside is safer.
lessons.tip: Fans and heaters use power or fuel. Always have an adult set them up and check them.

quiz.q: Why does a greenhouse need vents, even in the fall?
options: Sunny days can make it too hot

sources.t: Kentucky State University — Aquaponics Handbook (2021)
NMSU Extension — Important Water Quality Parameters in Aquaponics Systems (CR-680)

lessons.title: Balancing fish and plants in aquaponics
body: In aquaponics, fish food is really plant food. Fish eat it. Bacteria turn their waste into nitrate. So the food you feed each day sets how many plants the system can feed.

Growers keep three things in balance: fish, bacteria, and plants. Too few bacteria, and ammonia builds up and harms the fish. Too few plants, and nitrate piles up. Too many plants, and they go hungry.

Kentucky State University gives rules of thumb for raft beds. For leafy greens, feed about 40 to 60 grams of fish food a day for each square meter of plants. A square meter is about 11 square feet. For fruit crops like tomatoes, feed 60 to 100 grams. Keep fish to half a pound or less per gallon of water. Grown fish eat about 1 to 3 percent of their body weight each day. Gravel beds get 25 to 40 percent less food.
Your water tests show the balance. If ammonia or nitrite climbs, feed less and add air. If nitrate stays low and plants look pale, there may be too many plants for the fish.
lessons.tip: Weigh the fish food each day. Write it down next to your water test results so you can spot trends.

quiz.q: What happens if there are too many plants for the fish?
options: The fish grow twice as fast
The plants run short of food

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Understanding nitrogen in soils
WSU Extension — A Home Gardener's Guide to Soils and Fertilizers
University of Delaware Cooperative Extension — Nitrogen Cycling in Agriculture

lessons.title: The nitrogen cycle in garden soil
body: Plants need nitrogen to build leaves. The air is full of nitrogen gas, but plants can't use the gas. Nitrogen has to change form before roots can take it in. It moves in a loop called the nitrogen cycle.

Step one is fixing. A few kinds of bacteria can grab nitrogen gas and change it. Rhizobia bacteria live in small lumps, called nodules, on the roots of beans, peas, and clover. The plant gives the bacteria energy. The bacteria give the plant nitrogen.

Step two is mineralizing. Most soil nitrogen is locked up in dead plants, compost, and old roots. Roots can't use it yet. When the soil warms up, microbes eat that old matter. They set free ammonium, and ammonium is plant food.

Step three is nitrifying. In warm, damp soil with air in it, other microbes turn ammonium into nitrite, then nitrate. Nitrate is plant food too. It is the same two-step change that cleans fish water in aquaponics. It slows way down when soil is colder than 50°F.

Nitrogen can also leave. Nitrate does not stick to soil, so lots of rain or too much water can wash it down past the roots. That is called leaching. Sandy soil loses the most this way. In soggy soil with no air, microbes turn nitrate back into gas. That is called denitrifying. It can happen fast when warm soil stays soaked for two or three days. When we pick crops, we take nitrogen away too.
So the cycle leaks. Gardeners add nitrogen back with compost, fertilizer, or bean-family cover crops. They also try not to water more than plants need.
lessons.tip: Grow peas, beans, or clover in a bed. Their root bacteria add nitrogen for the next crop.

quiz.q: Which soil loses nitrate to leaching most easily?

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing beans in home gardens

lessons.title: Grow bush beans
body: Bush beans are easy to grow. They stand up on their own and get about two feet tall. They do not need a pole or a fence.
Wait until the soil is warm. Bean seeds in cold soil may rot. Push each seed about one inch deep. Space the seeds four inches apart.

Beans like about one inch of water each week from rain or a hose. Pick the pods while they are thin and snap easily. Do it before the beans inside make bumps. Keep picking, and the plants may make more pods.
lessons.tip: Plant a short row of bush beans every two weeks. Then you can pick beans all summer.

quiz.q: When should you pick snap beans?
options: After the pods turn dry and brown
Before the beans inside make bumps

sources.t: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook — 8. Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
Utah State University Extension — How to Monitor (Vegetable IPM)

lessons.title: Making a pest plan with IPM
body: IPM stands for integrated pest management. It means you use many tools against pests, and sprays come last. NC State Extension splits an IPM plan into five steps.

Step one is to monitor. Look at your plants often, like once a week. Check the tops and bottoms of leaves, the stems, and the fruit. Step two is to identify. Find out what the bug or problem really is. Many bugs are helpers, not pests.

Step three is to assess. Ask if the damage is too much. The amount of damage you can live with is called a threshold. Below it, you do nothing. Plants can lose some leaves and still grow fine. But pests multiply, so act before the damage reaches your limit.

Step four is to act. Pick the choice that works, costs little, and is the least toxic. Hand-picking or a row cover often comes first. An adult should handle any spray. Step five is to evaluate. Did it work? If not, change the plan.
lessons.tip: Keep a pest notebook. Write the date, the plant, what you saw, how many, and what you did. Next year you can spot patterns.

quiz.q: In IPM, what is a threshold?
options: The amount of damage you can live with

sources.t: Clemson HGIC — How Much to Grow: Planning for Year-Round Garden Productivity
NMSU Cooperative Extension — 4 Season Vegetable Gardening

lessons.title: Succession planting math
body: Succession planting means you plant small batches a few weeks apart. That way you don't get one huge harvest all at once. It also spreads out the risk if one batch fails.

Start with two numbers. Days to maturity is how long a crop takes from planting to picking. Harvest length is how long it keeps giving food. Clemson Extension lists snap beans at 50 to 60 days, with about 3 weeks of picking.

Fast crops get short gaps between batches. NMSU Extension lists 7 days for radishes and baby greens, 10 days for bush beans, and 14 days for beets. The gap should be shorter than the harvest length, so a new batch is ready as the old one fades.

Then count back from your first fall frost date. Your last batch needs enough days left to grow. Bush beans need about 50 to 60 days, so the last sowing should be at least 8 or 9 weeks before frost. Give it more time if you want the full 3 weeks of picking.
lessons.tip: Write each sowing date on a calendar. Mark the date for the next batch right away.

quiz.q: Which crop needs the shortest gap between plantings?

sources.t: Colorado State Univ. Extension — The Living Soil
Clemson HGIC — Why Does Soil Health Matter? Starting with Soil Organisms

lessons.title: The soil food web: who eats whom
body: Soil life forms a food web. Small living things become food for bigger ones. As they eat, plant food moves through the web and back to the roots.

It starts with plants. Leaves catch sunlight and make sugar. Roots leak some of that sugar into the soil. Bacteria and fungi near the roots feed on it. In return, they help the plant get nitrogen and other food. Bacteria and fungi also break down dead leaves and roots.

Next come the eaters. Protozoa are tiny living things with just one cell. They mostly eat bacteria. Bacteria hold more nitrogen than protozoa need, so protozoa let the extra go as ammonium. Ammonium is plant food. Nematodes are tiny round worms. Most eat bacteria, fungi, or other nematodes, but a few eat roots. Mites, springtails, and centipedes eat fungi, worms, or each other.

Some fungi join with roots. These pairs are called mycorrhizae. The fungus threads reach far out for water and food and trade them for sugar. They also make a glue called glomalin. It sticks clay bits into crumbs, which leaves room for air and water.

Your choices change the web. Tilling breaks fungus threads and crumbs, so mulch is a gentler way to stop weeds. Soggy soil harms soil life. Sprays you don't need can harm the helpers. Store-bought microbes are often not needed. Colorado State says most soils already have them, and they grow fast once food and water show up.
lessons.tip: Feed the web with compost and leaf mulch. Keep the soil covered and damp, but not soggy.

quiz.q: How do protozoa help feed plants?
options: They let go of extra nitrogen after eating bacteria

sources.t: University of Maryland Extension — Understanding Your Soil Test Report

lessons.title: Reading a soil test report
body: A soil test is a lab check of your soil. The report shows how much plant food is there. It also shows pH, organic matter, and what to add.

pH tells how sour or sweet soil is. The scale goes from 0 to 14, and 7 is in the middle. Most vegetables grow best from 5.5 to 7.0. Blueberries like 4.5 to 5.5. pH changes which foods roots can get. Below 6.0, phosphorus sticks to iron and aluminum. Above 7.3, it sticks to calcium. Either way, roots get less.

Many reports show two pH numbers. Soil pH is the acid in the soil right now. Buffer pH shows acid that is stored on clay and organic matter. The lower the buffer pH, the more lime it takes to raise the pH. So clay soil needs more lime than sandy soil. Lime raises pH, and sulfur lowers it.

Phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) each get a rating. If one says optimum or high, adding more will not help. Extra phosphorus can wash into streams. There it feeds algae, and when they die, the water loses the oxygen fish need.

CEC stands for cation exchange capacity. It shows how well soil holds on to foods like potassium and calcium. Clay and organic matter raise it. The University of Maryland says to add organic matter if CEC is below 10. Organic matter is measured by weight, so even rich soil may show less than 5 percent. Healthy soil has 2 percent or more.
The report may list fertilizer as pounds per 1,000 square feet. Pick a fertilizer whose N-P-K numbers come close to that mix, or use single foods. An adult should handle lime, sulfur, and fertilizer.
lessons.tip: Keep your reports in a folder. Comparing them over the years shows if your compost and lime are working.

quiz.q: Your report says phosphorus is optimum. What should you do?
options: Add lime to lower the pH

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — Late-season harvest in the vegetable garden
Nebraska Extension — Growing and harvesting tomatoes

lessons.title: Save green tomatoes before frost
body: Frost kills tomato plants. But you can save the green tomatoes that are still on the vine.
Pick them the day before frost comes. Choose big, firm ones that look pale green or a little pink. Small, dark green ones will not ripen well.
Pull off the stems. Wipe the tomatoes clean and dry. Set them in one layer in a cool, dark spot. Look at them every few days. Throw out any that get soft or rot.
Do not put green tomatoes in the fridge. Cold stops them from turning red.
lessons.tip: Want them to ripen faster? Put a few in a closed paper bag with an apple. The apple gives off a gas that helps them ripen.

quiz.q: Which green tomatoes are most likely to ripen inside?

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Bringing houseplants back inside
Washington State University Pestsense — Spider mites

lessons.title: Bring plants inside without bugs
body: Some potted plants spend summer outside and come in for winter. Tiny bugs can ride in with them. Inside, the bugs can spread fast.

Before you bring a plant in, look under its leaves. Then give it a bath. Ask an adult to help mix a little mild dish soap in water. Wash the tops and bottoms of the leaves, and rinse. Let the soapy water soak the soil, too.
Once inside, keep the plant away from your other plants for about a month. Check it each time you water.
lessons.tip: Bring plants in before nights get colder than about 50°F. Many potted plants get hurt by the cold.

quiz.q: What should you do with a plant you just brought inside?
options: Keep it away from other plants for a while
Put it right next to your other plants

sources.t: UC IPM — Fungus gnats (Pest Notes)
University of Minnesota Extension — Insects on indoor plants

lessons.title: Stop fungus gnats in pots
body: Fungus gnats are tiny black flies. You may see them walk on the soil of potted plants or seed trays. The flies do not bite. Their babies are the problem. These babies are called larvae. They look like tiny clear worms with shiny black heads. They live in wet soil and eat fungus and rotting bits. They can also chew on roots.

The main fix is to keep the soil drier. Let the top of the soil dry out before you water again. Use pots with holes in the bottom. Never let a pot sit in a puddle. Do not add unfinished compost to potting soil. Wet, rotting stuff is where the flies lay eggs.
Yellow sticky cards catch the grown flies. They show you how many gnats you have. But they will not stop the babies in the soil.

If the gnats keep coming back, an adult can water the soil with a product made from Bti. Bti is a germ that kills the larvae. Read and follow the label. A plant with lots of gnats can go into fresh, clean potting mix.
lessons.tip: Water seed trays from the bottom for a few minutes, then dump out the extra water. The top stays drier.

quiz.q: What do yellow sticky cards do for fungus gnats?
options: Kill the larvae in the soil
Catch the grown flies so you can count them

sources.t: UC IPM — Voles (Pest Notes)
Nebraska Extension — Controlling Vole Damage (G887)

lessons.title: Keep voles out of the garden
body: Voles are small, chubby rodents. They look like mice, but they have short tails and tiny eyes. They eat roots, bulbs, and vegetables. In fall and winter, they may chew the bark off young trees.

Look for their paths. Voles make little trails in the grass that link holes about two inches wide. Thick grass, weeds, and mulch hide the trails and keep voles safe. Voles do not like to eat out in the open.
So take away their cover. Keep the grass short near the garden. Keep a strip with no weeds around the beds. Pull thick mulch back from the stems of plants.

Then build a wall they cannot get past. Use wire mesh with holes a quarter inch wide or smaller. Bury the bottom 6 to 10 inches deep so they cannot dig under. Let the top stand at least 12 inches high. Voles do not climb well. Wire cages can guard young trees too.
Traps can help when there are only a few voles. Traps can hurt fingers, so an adult should set them and check them.
lessons.tip: Pull back the grass along a trail. Fresh grass bits and droppings mean voles are using it now.

quiz.q: How deep should you bury a wire fence to stop voles?
options: It does not need to be buried

sources.t: SDSU Extension — Planting garlic
University of Vermont — Vegetable and Berry Factsheet: Garlic

lessons.title: Garlic timing: roots now, leaves later
body: Garlic is planted in fall. It grows in two parts. First it grows roots in fall. Then it rests in the cold. In spring it grows leaves and a bulb.

Garlic needs cold to make a good bulb. The University of Vermont says it needs about two months near 40°F. That cold tells the plant to split into cloves. This is why fall planting works best in places with cold winters. Spring garlic often stays small.

Timing is a trade-off. Plant too early, and green leaves may come up in fall. Then winter can kill them. Plant too late, and the roots do not have time to grow before the ground freezes. A good sign is soil that is about 50°F four inches down. In many places, that is two or three weeks after the first frost. Use a soil thermometer, not just the date. A warm fall can fool the calendar.
Plant each clove with the root end down and the skin on. Set it a few inches deep. Deeper cloves stay safer from hard freezes.

Frost heave is when soil freezes, thaws, and freezes again. Each time it swells and shrinks. That can push cloves up out of the ground. Once the soil has frozen, add 6 to 8 inches of straw or shredded leaves. The mulch keeps the soil from flipping between frozen and thawed.
Mulch is not always good, though. In a wet spring, thick mulch keeps soil too wet. That can help disease. Pull it back from the plants so the soil can dry.
lessons.tip: Mix compost into the bed before planting. Skip extra fertilizer on planting day. The cloves need roots first, not leaves.

quiz.q: Why add straw to garlic after the soil freezes?
options: To make leaves come up in fall
To stop freezing and thawing from pushing cloves up
To warm the soil so it never freezes

sources.t: NMSU Extension — Important Water Quality Parameters in Aquaponics Systems (CR-680)

lessons.title: How fish poop becomes plant food
body: In aquaponics, fish and plants share the same water. Fish eat. Then they make a waste called ammonia. Most of it comes out of their gills. Old food and poop rot and make more. Too much ammonia makes fish sick.
Tiny living things called bacteria help out. They are too small to see. One kind eats the ammonia and makes nitrite. Nitrite is bad for fish too. A second kind eats the nitrite and makes nitrate.
Nitrate is food for plants! The roots drink it up. That cleans the water. Then the clean water flows back to the fish.
lessons.tip: Do not give the fish too much food. Old food rots in the water and makes more ammonia.

quiz.q: Which one is food for the plants?

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing beans in home gardens
Washington State University Extension — Growing Dry Beans in Home Gardens (FS135E)

lessons.title: Grow beans you can keep all year
body: Some beans are not picked green. You let them dry on the plant. These are dry beans, like black beans and pinto beans.
Plant the seeds after the soil is warm. Give them full sun. Then let the pods grow old. They turn brown and dry. Shake a pod. If the beans rattle, they are ready.
If cold rain is coming, pull up the whole plant. Hang it upside down inside to finish drying.
Open the dry pods by hand. Or put them in a sack and stomp on it. Keep the beans in a closed jar in a dark, dry place.
lessons.tip: Stomping the bean sack is a great job for kids. Pour the beans out on a windy day so the bits of pod blow away.

quiz.q: How can you tell dry beans are ready to pick?
options: The beans rattle in a dry pod

sources.t: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension) — Cilantro / Coriander
University of Maryland Extension — Cilantro/Coriander
NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Coriandrum sativum

lessons.title: Cilantro leaves and coriander seeds
body: Cilantro is an herb that likes cool weather. Its leaves taste fresh. Its seeds have a new name. They are called coriander.
Plant the seeds right in the garden in early spring. Plant more again in late summer. Cilantro does not like to be moved. It has one long root.
Hot days make cilantro bolt. That means it grows tall and makes flowers. The leaves stop being good. But the flowers feed helpful bugs.
Let some plants keep going. The flowers turn into round seeds. When the seeds turn light brown, cut the stems. Dry them inside. Then rub out the seeds.
lessons.tip: Plant a few seeds every two or three weeks. Then you will have new leaves for longer.

quiz.q: What do we call the seeds of the cilantro plant?

sources.t: University of Maryland Extension — Spotted Lanternfly in Home Gardens
Penn State Extension — Spotted Lanternfly Management Guide

lessons.title: Spotted lanternfly: what to do
body: The spotted lanternfly is a bug from Asia. It came to Pennsylvania in 2014. Now it lives in many states. It does not bite or sting.
It drinks sap from plants. Grapes are hurt the most. It also likes a weed tree called tree-of-heaven. As it feeds, it drips a sweet goo. Black mold can grow on the goo.

Know it at each stage. Young ones are black with white spots. Older young ones are red with white spots. Adults have gray wings with black spots. Their back wings are bright red. In fall, females lay eggs in flat gray patches. The patches look like dried mud. They can be on trees, rocks, cars, or grills.

You do not need to spray. Sprays can hurt bees and other good bugs. Home remedies like vinegar or dish soap sprays can hurt plants and animals too. Instead, squash the bugs. Or knock them into a cup of soapy water. Scrape egg patches into a bag and crush them.
Before you drive out of an area that has them, check your car and gear. If you find one where they have not been seen yet, take a photo and report it to your state's farm agency.
lessons.tip: Use an old plastic card to scrape off egg patches. Wear gloves. Make sure it is a lanternfly egg patch first, since some good bugs lay eggs on bark too.

quiz.q: What is the best way to deal with spotted lanternflies at home?
options: Squash them or scrape off their eggs
Leave out sweet goo for them

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Fire blight
Colorado State University Extension PlantTalk — Fireblight

lessons.title: Fire blight on apples and pears
body: Fire blight is a plant sickness. It is caused by bacteria, which are tiny living things. It hits apple and pear trees most. It can hit crabapples and some shrubs too.
Look for young shoots that wilt and bend down like a hook. The leaves turn brown or black but stay on the twig. The tree can look burned by fire. That is how it got its name.

Here is the science. The bacteria spend winter in cankers. A canker is a dark, sunken sore on the bark. In warm, wet spring weather, the canker leaks a sticky, sweet ooze. Bees and other bugs visit the ooze. They carry the bacteria to flowers. Rain splash and tools can spread it too. The bacteria get in through flowers and small cuts. Then they move inside the branch.
An adult can cut off a sick branch. Cut at least 12 inches below the sick part, into healthy wood. Take the cut branches away from the tree.
Fast, soft new growth gets sick more easily. So do not prune too hard. Skip extra nitrogen fertilizer. For new trees, pick kinds that resist fire blight.
lessons.tip: Pruning in late winter, when the tree is asleep, is safest. If you cut a sick tree in spring or summer, clean the blades between cuts. Use rubbing alcohol or a bleach mix, with adult help.

quiz.q: How do bees help fire blight spread?
options: They carry bacteria from the ooze to flowers

sources.t: Purdue Extension — HO-324: Cover Crops in the Home Garden
Iowa State University Extension — How to Terminate Cover Crops in the Vegetable Garden
Washington State University Extension — Methods for Successful Cover Crop Management in Your Home Garden

lessons.title: Cover crops: pick, grow, and stop them
body: A cover crop is a plant you grow to feed and guard the soil, not to eat. Most are sown in late summer or early fall, after the garden is picked.

Each kind does a different job. Grasses, like oats and cereal rye, make lots of roots and leaves. They hold soil in place. They soak up food left in the soil so rain does not wash it away. Legumes, like clover, peas, and hairy vetch, add nitrogen. Bacteria live in bumps on their roots. The bacteria pull nitrogen from the air. When the roots break down, the garden can use it. A mix of a grass and a legume gives you some of both.
Some cover crops die in the winter cold on their own. Oats and oilseed radish often do. That makes spring easy. Cereal rye lives through winter. It must be stopped in spring.

Timing is a trade-off. The plant gets bigger right up to the time it flowers. Bigger means more for the soil. But you must stop it before it makes seeds. If not, it becomes a weed. A good time is when about half the flowers are open.

Grasses stopped late turn tough and stringy. As soil life breaks them down, it uses up nitrogen for a while. Your next crop can run short. This is called nitrogen tie-up. Stopping earlier helps. So does growing a legume with the grass.
Fresh cover crop bits can also keep small seeds from sprouting. So wait two to four weeks after you cut it before you plant. Big transplants, like squash, can go into the cut plants used as mulch.
lessons.tip: To stop a cover crop, mow it high first, then mow again low. A string trimmer works for small beds. Get an adult to run the mower.

quiz.q: Why stop a cover crop when about half its flowers are open?
options: It has grown big but has not made seeds yet
That is when it adds the most weeds
It needs to be cut before it grows roots

sources.t: University of Wisconsin Extension — Beginning Vegetable Garden Basics: Site Selection and Soil Preparation
NDSU Extension — Pickin' Patch: Feeding Big Appetites from Small Spaces
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Planning the Vegetable Garden

lessons.title: Pick a sunny garden spot
body: Most food plants need sun. Pick a spot that gets at least six hours of full sun each day. Eight or more is even better.
Watch the spot on a sunny day. See where the shade from trees and houses falls.
Stay away from trees. Their roots take water and food from your plants. Do not pick a low spot where water sits after rain. Cold air sinks there too.
Pick a spot close to a hose, so watering is easy.
lessons.tip: Ask an adult to check for pipes or wires under the ground before you dig.

quiz.q: How many hours of sun do most food plants need each day?

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — How to Kill Grass to Create a New Garden Bed
University of Maryland Extension — Lawn (Turfgrass) Removal Methods
University of Wisconsin Extension — Beginning Vegetable Garden Basics: Site Selection and Soil Preparation

lessons.title: Clear the grass for a new garden
body: Grass and weeds must go before you plant. If not, they will grow back and fight your plants.
One easy way is to cover them. Mow the grass short. Lay flat cardboard on top. Take off all tape first. Make the edges overlap so no light gets in. Wet it, then put compost or leaves on top.
With no light, the grass dies. This takes weeks or months. Fall is a great time to start for a spring garden.
You can also dig the grass out with a flat shovel. Shake the good soil off the roots.
lessons.tip: A big tarp held down with bricks works too. Take it off once the grass is brown.

quiz.q: Why does cardboard kill grass?

sources.t: University of Georgia CAES — Great Garden Soils Don't Come Naturally
NDSU Extension — Pickin' Patch: Feeding Big Appetites from Small Spaces
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Soil Preparation

lessons.title: Is the soil ready to dig?
body: Do not dig or till soil when it is wet. Wet soil turns into hard lumps. They can stay hard all year.
Try the squeeze test. Dig down a few inches. Pick up a handful of soil and squeeze it. Then open your hand.
If the soil falls apart, it is ready. If it stays in a sticky mud ball, it is too wet. Wait a few dry days and test again.
If the soil is dry like dust, it is too dry. Water it and wait a day.
lessons.tip: If soil sticks to your shovel, it is too wet to work.

quiz.q: You squeeze soil and it stays in a mud ball. What should you do?

sources.t: University of Arkansas Extension — Prepare Your Garden
University of Wisconsin Extension — Beginning Vegetable Garden Basics: Site Selection and Soil Preparation
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Soil Preparation

lessons.title: Dig or till the soil
body: Roots like soft soil. Loose soil lets roots, air, and water move down.
For a small garden, use a spade or a garden fork. Turn the soil about six to eight inches deep. That is about as deep as your hand is long.
For a big garden, an adult can use a tiller.
Spread compost on top and mix it in. Break up big lumps. Pull out roots, rocks, and sticks. Then rake the top smooth and flat, so small seeds can sprout.
lessons.tip: Only adults should run a tiller. Stay far back while it is on.

quiz.q: About how deep should you turn the soil?

sources.t: Oregon State University Extension — How do I place my garden rows to promote the best growth?
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Planning the Vegetable Garden

lessons.title: Lay out rows and paths
body: Rows keep a garden neat. They help you know where you planted seeds.
Push a stick in the ground at each end of the row. Tie a string tight between them. Plant along the string, so the row is straight.
Leave paths between rows, so you can walk and pick. Read the seed packet to see how far apart to make rows.
If you can, run rows north to south. Put tall plants, like corn, at the north end. Then they will not shade the short plants.
lessons.tip: Walk only on the paths. Feet press the soil hard where roots need to grow.

quiz.q: Where should tall plants go so they do not shade short ones?

sources.t: UConn Home & Garden Education Center — Garden Beds
Utah State University Extension — Tips for Growing Garden Vegetables: Soil Preparation
University of Minnesota Extension — Reducing Tillage Intensity in Vegetable Crops
University of Maryland Extension — Lawn (Turfgrass) Removal Methods

lessons.title: Till, no-till, broadfork, or double dig?
body: There is more than one way to loosen soil. Each has good points and bad points.

Tilling mixes the soil fast. It is a quick way to turn under dead sod and compost on a new plot. But too much tilling breaks the soil crumbs apart. It brings weed seeds up to sprout. Never till wet soil.

No-till means you do not turn the soil. You smother weeds and pile compost on top, then plant in it. Soil life is left alone. It takes more compost and more time to start. It works best on small plots.
A broadfork is a wide fork with long teeth and two handles. You push it in and rock it back. It loosens soil but does not flip the layers. It is hard work, so it fits small gardens.

Double digging loosens soil two spades deep. Dig a trench and set the top soil aside. Loosen the soil in the bottom with a fork. Then move over and do it again. Save it for hard, heavy clay. Sandy soil does not need it.
lessons.tip: New garden on hard clay? Double dig once. After that, a fork or broadfork each year is often enough.

quiz.q: What does a broadfork do that a tiller does not?
options: It loosens soil without flipping the layers

sources.t: University of Wisconsin Extension — Beginning Vegetable Garden Basics: Site Selection and Soil Preparation
NDSU Extension — Pickin' Patch: Feeding Big Appetites from Small Spaces
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Soil Preparation
K-State Research and Extension — Fall Garden Soil Preparation

lessons.title: Feed the ground before you plant
body: A new garden spot needs food and good crumbs. The best time to add them is before you plant.
Start with a soil test. It tells you the pH and how much food is there. It also says what to add. See the lesson How to take a soil test. Most food plants like a pH of about 6 to 7.

Next, add compost. Spread two to three inches on top. Mix it into the top few inches of soil. Do this about a month before planting. Compost helps sandy soil hold water. It helps clay soil drain. See Soil amendments: how much compost to add.
Add lime or fertilizer only if the test says so. Mix it in when you add the compost. Adding food after plants are in the ground is harder.
Then rake the top smooth. Now the bed is ready when the weather is right.
lessons.tip: Fall is a great time to test, so the results are back before spring.

quiz.q: When is the best time to add lime the soil test asks for?
options: Before planting, mixed in with compost

lessons.title: Raised rows for wet ground
body: Some ground stays wet a long time. This happens most on flat clay soil. Roots need air, and wet soil has little air.
A raised row helps. Use a hoe, rake, or tiller to pull soil up into a long, low hump. The top should be about 10 to 12 inches wide. Water drains off the hump and into the low path beside it.
A raised row is not a raised bed with walls. It is just the ground's own soil, piled up. You can make new ones each year. See the lesson Raised beds for the kind with sides.
Plant on the top of the row. Walk only in the low paths. Then the soil you plant in stays soft.
If your ground drains well, you may not need raised rows at all. Flat rows are fine there.
lessons.tip: After a hard rain, look at your garden. If water sits in puddles, raised rows can help.

quiz.q: Why do raised rows help on wet clay ground?

lessons.title: Fall or spring? A ground prep calendar
body: You can get ground ready in fall or in spring. Fall is often better, but not on every spot.

Fall work has some wins. Winter cold helps. Water in the soil freezes and thaws again and again. This breaks big lumps into small crumbs. Spring soil is often wet for weeks. If you wait, you may be tempted to dig mud. That makes clods that last all season.
Fall work has a risk too. Bare soil can wash away in winter rain. This is worst on a slope. So cover the soil. Sow a cover crop, like cereal rye. Or spread a thick layer of leaves.

Here is a plan. In early fall, clear grass and take a soil test. In mid fall, add compost and anything the test calls for. Loosen the soil and leave it rough. Then plant a cover crop or mulch. Over winter, plan your rows on paper.

In early spring, do the squeeze test each week. When the soil crumbles, open it and rake it smooth. Plant cool crops first. Wait until after your last frost for warm crops. See Frost dates vs. hardiness zones.
lessons.tip: On a hill, do not leave soil bare all winter. Keep it covered with plants or mulch.

quiz.q: How does winter help soil that was dug in fall?
options: Freezing and thawing break lumps into crumbs

lessons.title: Slopes, drainage, and contour rows
body: Water runs downhill. On a slope, it can carry your best soil away. That is called erosion. The top layer of soil holds the most food, so losing it hurts.

Rows that run up and down the hill make little ditches. Water races down them and takes soil with it. Instead, run rows across the slope. Follow the shape of the hill, so each row stays level. These are called contour rows. Each one is like a small dam. It slows the water so it can soak in.
On a steep slope, rows are not enough. Build terraces. A terrace is a flat step cut into the hill. Rocks or boards hold up the low side.
Stop water before it reaches the garden too. Send water from roofs and driveways away from the hill. A shallow trench at the top can carry it off.
The bottom of a hill has its own problem. Water and cold air both collect there. Soil stays wet and cold in spring. Raised beds or raised rows help in spots like that.
lessons.tip: Cover the paths between rows with straw or leaves. Bare paths on a slope wash away first.

quiz.q: Which way should rows run on a slope?
options: Straight up and down the hill
Across the hill, along its shape

lessons.title: Planning a large plot
body: A big garden needs a plan before the first dig. The key question is this: where will feet and wheels go?
Every step or tire presses the soil. Pressed soil has fewer air spaces. Roots and water have a hard time moving down. So plan beds and paths on purpose, and keep them the same each year.
For hand work, make beds about three to four feet wide. You can reach the middle from either side. You never need to step in the bed. Paths take the traffic.

For a tiller or tractor, measure the tool first. Set the row spacing so the wheels always fit in the same paths. Mark your rows the same way every year. This is called controlled traffic. The paths get hard, but the beds stay soft.
There are trade-offs. Wide paths waste some ground. Narrow ones are hard to work in. Small gardens can use narrow paths. Big ones need room to turn a tractor at the ends.

Also plan for water and rotation. Put the hose or drip line where it can reach every bed. Split the plot into blocks, so crop families can move each year. Put perennial crops, like asparagus, at the side, where tillage will not reach them.
lessons.tip: Draw the plot on paper. Mark every bed, path, and turn row before you dig.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of controlled traffic?
options: Wheels and feet stay on the same paths, so beds stay soft

lessons.title: Compaction, hardpan, and subsoiling
body: Soil is not solid. About half of good soil is space between bits of earth. Those spaces, called pores, hold air and water. Compaction means weight squeezes the pores shut.

Wetness makes it worse. Damp soil is the easiest to squash. Dry soil has small air pockets that act like cushions. That is why the squeeze test matters. Most of the pressing happens on the first trip over the soil.

Some compaction is deep. A plow or tiller run at the same depth year after year can leave a hard layer just below. So can heavy wheels. That layer is called a hardpan. Roots stop at it and spread sideways. Water pools on top. In a dry year, plants cannot reach water deeper down. Pressed soil also stays wet and cold longer in spring.
To find a hardpan, push a long wire rod into damp soil. Feel where it suddenly gets hard. Or dig a hole and look for roots that turn flat.

A subsoiler is a long steel shank pulled by a tractor. It breaks a deep hardpan. Use it only when the soil at that depth is dry enough to crumble. Wet soil just smears. Go only two or three inches below the hard layer. Research results are mixed. The soil can pack again with more traffic.

So stopping compaction beats fixing it. Stay off wet soil. Keep wheels in the same lanes. Keep tire pressure right, and do not haul heavy loads. Change tillage depth now and then, or till less. Deep roots of cover crops and compost help too. In a small garden, double digging or a broadfork does the same job by hand.
lessons.tip: Leave one strip without subsoiling. Compare it at harvest to see if the work paid off.

quiz.q: Why should you not subsoil when the deep soil is wet?
options: The steel smears wet soil instead of cracking it

sources.t: University of Delaware Cooperative Extension — Non-chemical pest control for brassicas

lessons.title: Stop worms from eating cabbage
body: Holes in your cabbage, kale, or broccoli? A small green worm may be to blame. It is the cabbage worm. It hatches from eggs laid by a white butterfly.
Look under the leaves when plants are young. Pick off the green worms. Rub off the tiny yellow eggs too.

You can also cover the plants with light cloth called row cover. Put it on right after you plant. Hold the edges down so no butterfly can get in. These plants do not need bees to make food, so the cover can stay on until you pick.
After you pick your crop, clean up the old plants. Then the worms have no place to hide for winter.
lessons.tip: Some gardeners use a spray called Bt that only hurts worms like these. Always let an adult do any spraying.

quiz.q: Where do cabbage worms and their eggs hide?

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension Yard and Garden — Keeping squirrels from digging tulip bulbs
UNH Extension — How can I keep wildlife from eating my new bulbs?

lessons.title: Keep squirrels from digging bulbs
body: You plant tulip bulbs in fall. The next day, there are holes, and the bulbs are gone! Squirrels and other critters love to dig up fresh bulbs. Here is how to stop them.

First, plant deep. Put big bulbs like tulips, daffodils, and hyacinths 6 to 8 inches down. Put small bulbs like crocus and grape hyacinth 3 to 4 inches down. Press the soil firm with your hands. Then water it well. Deep, firm soil is harder to dig.

The best fix is a wire cover. Lay chicken wire or hardware cloth (a stiff wire mesh) over the bed. Set bricks on top to hold it. Take the wire off in early spring, before the leaves poke up. You can also bury bulbs inside a small wire cage. Ask an adult to help cut wire, since the ends are sharp.
Skip bone meal when you plant. Its smell can draw in animals that dig. Also mix in bulbs that critters do not like to eat. Daffodils, alliums, snowdrops, and grape hyacinths are good picks.
lessons.tip: Plant tulips with daffodils around them, and lay wire on top until spring.

quiz.q: When should you take the wire cover off a bulb bed?
options: In summer after the flowers fade
In early spring before the leaves come up

sources.t: UC Master Gardeners of San Luis Obispo County — Dahlias: digging, dividing, and storing
Ohio State University Extension, Erie County — Storing dahlia tubers over winter

lessons.title: Store dahlia tubers for winter
body: Dahlias grow from tubers. A tuber is a fat root that stores food. Where the ground freezes in winter, tubers left in the soil can freeze or rot. So in cold places, gardeners dig them up in fall. In mild places, they can often stay in the ground.

Wait for a hard frost to turn the leaves black. Cut the stems down to a short stub. Then lift the clump with a garden fork. Go slow so you do not cut the tubers. Even a small cut can let rot in. Ask an adult to help with the fork and any cutting tools.

Rinse off the dirt with a hose. Let the tubers dry for one or two days. Pick a spot with fresh air where it will not freeze. Next, lay them in a box so they do not touch. Cover them with a dry fill like peat moss, vermiculite, or wood shavings. Keep the box cool and dark, about 40 to 50 °F (4 to 10 °C).

Check the box once a month. Throw out any tuber that is soft or rotten. If you see mold, brush it off and move the box to a drier spot. If tubers look wrinkled, spray a light mist on the fill. Clean your cutting tools between plants so you do not spread germs.
lessons.tip: Write the name of each dahlia on a tag before you store it, so you know which is which in spring.

quiz.q: What should you do if a stored tuber looks wrinkled?
options: Lightly mist the fill around it
Put it in a hot, sunny window
Soak it in a bucket of water

NC State Extension — Destructive jumping earthworms

lessons.title: Jumping worms hurt garden soil
body: Not all worms help a garden. Jumping worms came from Asia. When you pick one up, it thrashes and wiggles like a snake. It may even drop part of its tail. These worms live near the top of the soil. They eat leaves and mulch fast.
They leave the soil loose and grainy. It looks like used coffee grounds. This soil dries out fast and has less plant food in it. Plants may grow poorly. The worms also push out the good earthworms.

There is no spray to kill them. So you remove them by hand. Pick them up and seal them in a trash bag. Or drop them in a jar of vinegar or rubbing alcohol. Ask an adult to help with these liquids. To find them, mix 1/3 cup of ground hot yellow mustard in 1 gallon of water. Pour it slowly on the soil. Worms will crawl up to the top. Keep pets from drinking the mix.

Stopping them is the best plan. Use your own leaves and compost. Heat kills the worms and their eggs at over 105 °F (41 °C). So if you buy mulch or compost, ask if it was heat treated. Buy plants with bare roots when you can. Do not share potted plants with your garden soil in them. Brush soil off tools and shoes.
The grown worms die after a hard frost. But tiny egg cases live through the winter. They hatch when the soil stays near 50 °F (10 °C) in spring.
lessons.tip: Look for the coffee-ground soil and snake-like wiggle in summer, when the worms are big.

quiz.q: What does soil with jumping worms look like?

sources.t: University of Wisconsin–Madison Extension Horticulture — When is the right time to plant vegetable seeds? Check soil temperature
University of Maryland Extension — Poor germination of vegetable seeds

lessons.title: Plant when the soil is warm enough
body: Most seed packs say to plant a set time before or after your last frost date. But that date is about the air. Seeds sit in the soil. Soil warms up and cools down much more slowly than air. A warm day in spring does not mean the soil is warm yet. So a soil test can tell you more than a calendar.

Use a soil thermometer to check. Take a reading at the same time each morning for three days in a row. Late morning, between 10 and noon, works well. Push it 2 inches down for seeds. Push it 4 to 6 inches down for plants you set out. Then take the average of the three days.

Cool weather crops can sprout in cold soil. Lettuce, peas, radish, carrots, beets, and spinach will sprout once the soil is above about 40 °F (4 °C). Warm weather crops need more heat. Beans, squash, and cucumbers will not sprout if the soil is below about 50 °F (10 °C). Corn and bean seeds can rot in soil that is cold and wet.

Some charts give a safer number to wait for. One Wisconsin chart lists peas at 50 °F, corn at 55 °F, tomato seed at 70 °F, and beans at 72 °F. In cold soil, seeds sprout slow and may grow weak. In warm soil, they come up fast and strong.

You can help soil warm up. Raised beds warm faster than flat ground. Clear plastic laid on the soil traps heat like a tiny greenhouse. Thick, light mulch does the reverse. It keeps soil cool. So pull mulch back in spring if you want the soil to warm. Even with warm soil, a late frost can still come. Keep a cover ready for young plants.
lessons.tip: Write down your soil readings each spring. Over a few years you will learn when your own soil warms up.

quiz.q: Why is soil temperature a better guide than air temperature for planting seeds?
options: Soil changes temperature more slowly, and seeds sit in the soil
Air is always colder than soil

lessons.title: Garden helpers and garden harmers
body: Soil is full of life. Some living things help plants. Some hurt them. Many do neither.
Bugs: Lady beetles eat aphids, so they help. White grubs eat plant roots, so they harm.

Worms: Most garden earthworms dig tunnels that let in air and water. But jumping worms are a pest in some places. They hurt the soil. A cutworm is not a real worm. It is a caterpillar that cuts young plants.
Microbes are living things too small to see. Many break down dead leaves into plant food. Some help roots get water. A few cause plant sickness, like wilt.
lessons.tip: Add compost and mulch to feed the helpers. Look closely before you call a bug bad.

quiz.q: What is a cutworm?
options: A caterpillar that cuts young plants
