lessons.title: Count heat, not days
body: Plants and bugs grow with heat. A warm spring wakes them up early. A cold spring makes them late. So the date on a calendar can fool you.
Gardeners count heat with growing degree days. Each plant or bug has a base temperature. Below that, it barely grows. Many bugs use 50°F as the base.

Here is how to count one day. Add the high and the low. Cut that in half. Then take away the base. A high of 75 and a low of 55 gives 65 on average. Take away 50 and you get 15 for that day. If the answer is below zero, call it zero.
Add the days up all season. The total tells you how far along things are. You do not have to do the math. Many university websites show degree days for your area.
lessons.tip: Look up degree days for your area online. Check the map each week in spring.

quiz.q: What does a degree day count?
options: How much heat has built up

sources.t: Illinois Extension — Growing Degree Days: A Tool for Smarter Gardening
Iowa State University Extension — Using Growing Degree Days to Manage the Home Garden

lessons.title: Time bug checks with degree days
body: Bugs are cold-blooded. Their bodies grow when the air is warm. This means a bug's life follows heat, not the calendar.

Experts have found how many degree days many pests need before they hatch or fly. In Illinois, Japanese beetle adults start to come out around 950 degree days. If your total is near that number, it is time to look for them.
This helps you compare years. One Illinois town had 1,320 degree days on June 24, 2025. A year before, it had 1,540 on the same date. So the bugs came later in 2025.

Different living things use different base temperatures. Some start just above freezing. Cool-season crops and early perennials often use 40°F. Many insects use 50°F. Heat lovers use 60°F or more. Pick the base that fits the thing you are tracking. Base 50 often starts on March 1. Base 32 often starts on January 1.
Acting at the right time works better than reacting after damage shows. Use degree days to know when to scout. Then look at your plants with your own eyes. Ask an adult before any spray.
lessons.tip: Write the date you first see a pest in your journal. Next year, compare it to the degree days.

quiz.q: Why do gardeners track degree days for pests?
options: To know the best time to scout and act

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — Using Growing Degree Days to Manage the Home Garden
Illinois Extension — Growing Degree Days: A Tool for Smarter Gardening

lessons.title: What degree days can and cannot tell you
body: Degree days turn weather into one running number. That number tracks heat. Plants and insects respond to heat. So the total can predict bloom, egg hatch, and adult flight better than a date can.

Scientists use the word phenology. It means the study of events that repeat each year, like leaf buds, flowers, and insect hatches. The dates move from year to year. But the events line up with heat totals much more closely.

This is why indicator plants work. Lilac bloom often matches the time certain pests come out. Crabapple bloom can signal when to time apple pest care. Both plants and pests react to the same heat, so one can warn you about the other.
The method has limits. It uses only air temperature. It ignores rain, soil moisture, day length, and harsh weather. A drought can slow a plant even when the totals look normal.
Your garden may also differ from the weather station. A shady corner is cooler. A brick wall or a city can be warmer. Different plant varieties and pest groups also grow at different speeds.
So use degree days as a guide, not a promise. Keep notes. Match what you see to the numbers. Over several years your notes will make the numbers more useful for your own yard.
lessons.tip: Pair degree days with a simple log: date, degree total, and what bloomed or hatched.

quiz.q: Which is a limit of degree days?

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — Growing Citrus Indoors
University of Maryland Extension — Growing Dwarf Citrus

lessons.title: Grow a lemon or lime tree in a pot
body: Some small citrus trees grow well in pots. Good choices are Meyer lemon, Persian lime, kumquat, and calamondin. A tree sold already grafted stays small. A tree grown from seed can get big and thorny.

Citrus needs lots of light. Give it 6 to 8 hours of direct sun a day. A south or west window is best. Use a grow light if the window is weak. In summer, once nights are warm, move it outside. Do it slowly, starting in part shade.
Water when the top 2 inches of soil feel dry. Use a pot with holes. Let extra water drain out, and empty the saucer. Too much water rots roots. Too little makes leaves fall.
Keep it warm. Days around 65 to 85°F are good. Frost can kill it. Dry winter air hurts it, so a humidifier near the plant helps.

Indoors, no bees visit the flowers. You can use a small dry paintbrush to move pollen from flower to flower. Fruit can take 6 to 9 months to ripen. Plant food should be used only when the tree is growing. Ask an adult to handle the fertilizer.
lessons.tip: Check the leaves each week for tiny bugs. Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth.

quiz.q: How can you help flowers make fruit on a citrus tree indoors?
options: Move pollen with a small brush
Keep it in a dark room

sources.t: K-State Research and Extension — Harvesting and roasting sunflower seeds

lessons.title: Harvest sunflower seeds
body: Sunflower seeds are ready late in the season. Birds love them, so cover the head early. When the petals turn brown, put a paper bag or cheesecloth over the head. Hold it with a rubber band. The cover also keeps ripe seeds from falling out.
How do you know the seeds are ready? The back of the head turns lemon yellow. The head faces down. Pull out a few seeds. They should be black with white stripes.
Cut the head. Ask an adult to help with the knife. Hang it upside down to dry, or set it in a paper sack. When it is dry, rub the seeds out gently.
lessons.tip: Empty shells mean the flowers were not pollinated. Plant near bees next year.

quiz.q: What color are ripe sunflower seeds?

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — How can I over-winter my geraniums indoors?

lessons.title: Keep geraniums alive in winter
body: Geraniums do not like frost. You can bring them inside before the first frost and keep them for next year.
Inside, some leaves may turn yellow and fall off. That is normal. The plant is getting used to its new home.
Put the pot in your sunniest window, or under a grow light. Keep the room cool, not hot. Water only when the top of the soil feels dry.
No sunny window? You can dig the plants up, shake off the dirt, and keep them in a paper bag in a cool, dry room. In March, cut them back and plant them in pots again.
lessons.tip: Too much water is the most common problem. Touch the soil first. If it feels damp, wait.

quiz.q: When should you water a geranium kept inside for winter?
options: When the top of the soil is dry

sources.t: UC Statewide IPM Program — White Rot
University of Maryland Extension — White Rot of Alliums in the Home Garden

lessons.title: Stop white rot in garlic and onions
body: White rot is a fungus. It hurts garlic, onions, and their plant family. The leaves turn yellow and die early. When you pull a bulb, you may see white fuzz. Later you may see tiny black dots that look like poppy seeds.
Those black dots are the big problem. They rest in the soil and wait. They can stay alive for many years, even with no garlic there. Cool, damp soil helps the fungus grow.

If you find white rot, pull the sick plants. Put them in the trash, not the compost. Do not plant garlic or onions in that bed for at least 4 or 5 years. Brush dirt off your tools and boots before you move to another bed.

Next time, start clean. Buy garlic that is sold as certified disease free. Do not plant garlic from the grocery store. It can carry the fungus without looking sick. Give each plant space so air can move. Raised beds can help too.
In hot, sunny summers, you can also cover the bed with clear plastic for 4 to 6 weeks. The sun heats the soil and kills much of the fungus. Ask an adult to help lay the plastic.
lessons.tip: Mark the sick bed on a map or sign so no one plants garlic or onions there by mistake.

quiz.q: Where should garlic plants with white rot go?
options: Back in the same bed next year

sources.t: Agriculture Victoria — Controlling Queensland fruit fly in home gardens

lessons.title: Keep fruit flies out of tomatoes and fruit
body: In parts of Australia, a pest called the Queensland fruit fly lays eggs inside fruit. Tomatoes and many kinds of fruit can be hit. The fruit may look fine on the outside. Inside, small maggots eat it. The flies get busy as spring warms up.

The best fix is a net. Use fine insect mesh that can take the sun. Put it over the plant after the flowers have been pollinated. Close it at the ground or tie it around the trunk so there are no gaps. Keep fruit from touching the net, because the fly can lay eggs through it. You can also put small bags over single fruit.

Keep the garden clean. Pick fruit as it gets ripe. Pick up fallen fruit every few days. Do not put bad fruit in the compost. To kill the maggots, seal it in a bag and freeze it for two days, or seal it in two bags and leave it in the sun for 14 days. Then put it in the rubbish bin.
Traps with a food lure can catch the female flies. Some gardeners also use bait sprays. An adult should do any spraying and follow the label.
lessons.tip: Other countries have their own fruit flies. Your local farm agency can tell you which ones live near you.

quiz.q: Why should fruit not touch the net?
options: The fly can lay eggs through the net

sources.t: NC State Extension — Manage Compost and Soil Contaminated with Broadleaf Herbicides in Gardens
K-State Research and Extension, Butler County — Herbicide in compost

lessons.title: When compost or manure hurts your plants
body: Sometimes new compost or manure makes plants sick. Tomato leaves curl and twist. Beans grow small and bent. One cause can be weed killer that stayed in the hay or grass. Cows and horses eat the hay. The weed killer passes through them and stays in the manure, even after composting.

This kind of weed killer is called persistent. That means it lasts a long time. It harms tomatoes, peppers, beans, peas, potatoes, lettuce, and many flowers. It does not hurt grass plants like corn, wheat, and onions.

You can test it with a simple bioassay. That word means using a plant as a tester. Fill some pots with the suspect soil and some with clean potting mix. Plant three pea or bean seeds in each. Grow them for two to three weeks. If the beans in the suspect soil curl or stay tiny, the soil likely has weed killer in it.

If the test fails, grow only corn, grass, or onions there for now. Pull the whole plants at the end of the season and put them in the trash, not the compost. Keep the soil warm and moist. Mix in clean compost. It often fades in about a year, but it can last longer in dry soil. Test again each year.
Need a garden sooner? Build a raised bed with a plastic or pond liner under it, then fill it with clean soil. Before you bring home manure, hay, or compost again, ask what was sprayed on the fields.
lessons.tip: Run a bean test on any new load of manure or compost before you spread it on the whole garden.

quiz.q: Which plant is safe to grow in soil with this kind of weed killer?

sources.t: UC Statewide IPM Program — Soil Solarization for Gardens & Landscapes
UC Statewide IPM Program — White Rot

lessons.title: Use the sun to clean sick soil
body: Some plant diseases live in the soil. White rot, Fusarium wilt, and Verticillium wilt are a few. Soil solarization uses sunlight to cook these pests. It uses no sprays. It leaves nothing behind.

Here is how it works. You cover moist soil with clear plastic. Sunlight passes through the plastic and warms the soil. The heat cannot get back out, much like a car in the sun. In hot places the top 2 inches can reach 108 to 140 °F. Deeper down it stays cooler. So it works best on pests in the top 6 inches.
Water matters. Wet soil carries heat better than dry soil. Wet soil also makes weak pests easier for good soil microbes to attack.

To do it, rake the bed smooth and pick out clods and old roots. Water it well. Lay clear plastic tight against the soil. Bury the edges in a shallow trench so wind cannot lift it. Clear plastic works better than black plastic, because black plastic soaks up the heat instead of passing it down. Leave it on for 4 to 6 weeks in the hottest, sunniest part of summer.

It has limits. It needs long, hot, sunny days, so it works best in warm, dry climates. Shade, wind, and clouds lower the heat. Some deep weeds and some heat-loving diseases survive. Small worms called nematodes can dig down to escape. Many helpful microbes live through it or come back fast.
After you take the plastic off, plant without digging deep. Deep digging can bring up weed seeds that the heat never reached. Ask an adult to help handle big sheets of plastic.
lessons.tip: Use a soil thermometer under the plastic to see how hot it really gets.

quiz.q: Why is clear plastic used instead of black for solarization?
options: Clear plastic lets sunlight through to heat the soil
Clear plastic keeps the soil dry

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing potatoes in home gardens
RHS — How to grow potatoes

lessons.title: Grow potatoes from seed potatoes
body: Potatoes do not grow from tiny seeds. You plant a piece of potato. Buy clean seed potatoes at a garden store. Store potatoes from the kitchen may carry sickness, or they may be treated so they will not sprout.
Each piece needs at least one eye. An eye is a small dent where a sprout comes out. Ask an adult to cut big ones with a clean knife. Let the pieces dry for a few days.
Plant them in a sunny spot when the soil warms in spring. Set them 3 to 5 inches deep and about a foot apart.
When the plants are about a foot tall, pile soil up around the stems. This is called hilling.
lessons.tip: Hilling keeps new potatoes in the dark. Sun turns them green, and green parts are not safe to eat.

quiz.q: Why do you pile soil up around potato plants?
options: To make the leaves grow faster
To keep the new potatoes in the dark

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing peas in home gardens
RHS — How to grow peas

lessons.title: Plant peas early in spring
body: Peas like cool weather. You can plant them in spring as soon as the ground thaws and is dry enough to dig. Young pea plants can live through a light frost.
Plant each seed about 1 inch deep and a few inches apart. Tall kinds climb, so give them a fence, net, or string to hold on to. Short kinds can lean on each other.
Peas stop making flowers and pods when the days get hot. That is why an early start helps.
Pick the pods when the peas inside are plump. Check every day. Peas turn hard and lose their sweet taste in just a few days. Cool them right after you pick them.
lessons.tip: Plant a few more seeds a week later. Then you will have peas to pick for longer.

quiz.q: What kind of weather do peas like best?

sources.t: University of Maryland Extension — Growing Sweet Potatoes in a Home Garden
RHS — How to grow sweet potatoes

lessons.title: Grow sweet potatoes from slips
body: Sweet potatoes first came from warm, tropical places. They are not close kin to regular potatoes. They are cousins of the morning glory flower. Frost hurts them. They need a long, warm season, about 3 to 4 months or more.

You do not plant seeds. You plant slips. A slip is a young shoot that grows out of an old sweet potato. You can buy slips, or grow your own. Set a sweet potato in damp sand or potting mix in a warm spot. Shoots come up in a few weeks. A slip can also grow roots in a glass of water.

Plant slips after the last frost, when the soil is warm, about 65°F. That is spring where you live. In the south half of the world, spring comes in the months that are fall up north. Give them full sun, at least 6 hours a day. A raised ridge of soil warms up fast and drains well. In cool places, a greenhouse or plant covers help.
Water well for the first two months. After that, the vines can take some dry weather.

Dig before frost. Cut the vines off first. Ask an adult to help with the digging fork. The skin bruises easily, so dig gently. Keep them somewhere warm for about a week so cuts heal and they get sweeter. This is called curing. Then store them at about 55 to 60°F, cool but not cold.
lessons.tip: Young sweet potato leaves are good to eat too. Cook them like spinach.

quiz.q: What do you plant to grow sweet potatoes?
options: Slips, the young shoots from an old sweet potato
Cut pieces with eyes, like potatoes

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing summer squash and zucchini in home gardens
University of Maryland Extension — Growing Summer Squash (Zucchini) in a Home Garden
Ohio State University Extension (Ohioline) — Growing Tomatoes in the Home Garden
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Tomato Challenges

lessons.title: Why flowers fall off without making fruit
body: A flower must get pollen to make fruit. Pollen is a fine yellow dust. It has to reach the part of the flower that turns into fruit. Then seeds start and the fruit swells. This is called fruit set. If it fails, the flower dries up and drops.

Squash, cucumbers, melons, and pumpkins have male and female flowers. A male flower sits on a thin stem. A female flower has a tiny fruit just under its petals. The first flowers are often all male. They soon drop off. That is normal. Bees must carry pollen from male to female flowers. Rain, cold, and cloudy days keep bees home. Bug sprays during bloom can kill bees. Take row covers off once flowers open.

Tomato flowers are not like that. Each one has both parts, so it can pollinate itself. Wind, a shake, or a buzzing bumblebee knocks the pollen loose. Heat and cold are the big problems. When nights stay below 55°F or above 75°F, or days pass 90°F, tomato flowers often drop. Often you just have to wait for better weather.
Other causes hurt fruit set too. Too much nitrogen fertilizer makes lots of leaves but little fruit. Too little sun or too little water can also cause it.
You can help. For squash, pick a male flower in the morning. Pull off its petals and dab its pollen on a female flower. For tomatoes, gently tap or shake the flower clusters.
lessons.tip: Look under the petals. A tiny fruit means a female flower. A thin stem means a male flower.

quiz.q: Your first squash flowers fall off. They have thin stems and no tiny fruit. What is going on?
options: They are male flowers, and that is normal

sources.t: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook — Chapter 3: Botany

lessons.title: How water moves up through a plant
body: Roots take in water from the soil. But most of it does not stay. About 90 of every 100 drops go back out into the air. Only about 10 are used to build the plant and run its cells. This loss of water is called transpiration.

Water moves up through thin tubes called xylem (say ZY-lum). They run from the root tips to the leaf tips. The water in them is one long, unbroken line. Leaves have tiny holes called stomata (say STO-ma-ta). As water leaves through these holes, it tugs the next bit of water up the tubes. The leaves pull water up from the roots, a bit like a straw.

This flow does key jobs. It carries minerals from the soil up to the leaves. It cools leaves as the water dries off. It helps move sugar and plant signals called hormones. It keeps cells full and firm, and firm cells hold the plant up. A wilted plant has cells that lost water and went soft.

Weather sets the speed. Bright light, heat, and wind make a plant lose water faster. Damp, humid air slows it down. Each hole has two guard cells around it, like two lips. In heat or drought they close the hole to save water. Wilting also saves some water, since limp leaves show less surface to the air.

But there is a trade-off. The same holes let in carbon dioxide, a gas in the air. Plants need it to make sugar from sunlight. Closed holes mean less food. So a wilted plant is not resting. It is making less food. Wilting again and again, with slow recovery, keeps plants small. That is why crops in a drought rarely reach full size.
Use this in the garden. Hot, sunny, windy days pull the most water. Deep watering and mulch help roots keep up.
lessons.tip: Feel the soil before a hot, windy day. If it is dry, water deeply so the roots can keep up.

quiz.q: Why does a plant make less food when it wilts?
options: Its stomata close, so less carbon dioxide gets in
Its flowers use up all the water

sources.t: Iowa State University Extension — How to Protect Trees and Shrubs from Animal Damage Over Winter

lessons.title: Keep rabbits and mice off young tree bark
body: In winter, food is hard to find. Rabbits and mice chew the bark of young trees and shrubs. Apple, pear, crabapple, raspberry, and rose plants get hit a lot.

Bark is like a skin. Just under it are thin tubes that carry water and food. If an animal eats the bark all the way around the trunk, the tubes are cut. This is called girdling. The top of the tree will die.

Stop it before it starts. Put a fence ring around each young trunk by early or mid November. Use chicken wire or hardware cloth. Make it 24 to 36 inches tall so it still works above deep snow. Pin the bottom to the ground so rabbits can't crawl under. For mice and voles, use a ring of 1/4 inch hardware cloth with the bottom 2 to 3 inches buried. Keep wood mulch at least 6 inches from the trunk, since mice hide in it. Take the rings off in spring, about April.

Already chewed? If the bark is gone all the way around, plan to replace the tree. If some bark is left, the tree often heals. Paint and wraps on the wound do not help. Cut a chewed shrub stem just below the damage in early spring.
lessons.tip: After a big snow, check the rings. Clear snow away if rabbits can reach over the top.

quiz.q: What does a winter fence ring around a young tree trunk do?
options: It stops rabbits from chewing the bark

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Gummy stem blight and black rot
NC State Extension — Gummy Stem Blight and Phoma Blight on Cucurbits

lessons.title: Squash that cracks and drips gum
body: Do your squash or melons have brown spots that crack and ooze a sticky, amber drip? That can be a fungus disease. On leaves and stems it is called gummy stem blight. On the fruit it is called black rot. Squash, pumpkins, cucumbers, and melons can all get it.

The fungus lives on old dead vines in the soil. Splashing water carries its spores up onto plants. It gets in through small cuts. Bites from cucumber beetles and aphids make those cuts. Some bad seed carries it too.

Here is how to fight it. At the end of the season, pull out sick vines and fruit. Throw them away. Do not leave them in the bed. Wait at least two years before you grow any squash family plant in that spot again. Water at the base of the plant, or use a drip line, so leaves stay dry. Buy clean seed, and never save seed from sick plants.
When you pick squash, handle it gently so you don't nick the skin. Store only fruit with no spots or cuts.
lessons.tip: Make a map of where you grew squash this year. Next year, plant them in a new spot.

quiz.q: Where does the gummy stem blight fungus wait between seasons?
options: On old dead vines in the soil

sources.t: Rutgers Master Gardeners — Fig Tree Winter Protection
Iowa State University Extension — How do I over-winter the common fig?

lessons.title: Help a fig tree live through a cold winter
body: Fig trees come from warm places. Where winters are mild, they keep growing all year. Where winters get very cold, like zone 6 and colder, they need help.

Here is the science. The stems and the roots can stand different amounts of cold. Fig stems are often hurt when it stays below 20°F. Even a tough kind, 'Chicago Hardy', loses stems near 10°F. But its roots in the ground can live to about 15 to 20 below zero. So a frozen fig often grows back from the roots. The new shoots grow fast, but they rarely make ripe figs that same year. Bad damage can take two seasons to fix.

So the goal is to keep the stems alive. Wait until the leaves fall and the tree is asleep in late fall. Then trim it to a size you can handle and tie the branches together. Wrap it in burlap, then thick brown paper, then tar paper. Pile soil around the base. Or build a chicken wire cage, fill it with straw or leaves, and cover the top so rain runs off. Do not use plastic. It traps wet air and can cause rot.

Other choices work too. Bend the branches down into a trench and bury them. Or grow the fig in a big pot, at least 15 gallons, and move it to a cool garage or basement. Take covers off after spring frost is over.
lessons.tip: Pick a cold-tough kind like 'Chicago Hardy', 'Brown Turkey', or 'Celeste'. Plant it by a south-facing wall for extra warmth.

quiz.q: Why does a fig that froze to the ground often grow back?
options: Its roots can stand much more cold than its stems
Figs grow new seeds every winter

sources.t: University of Wisconsin–Madison Extension — Blossom End Rot
University of Minnesota Extension — Tomato disorders
University of Maryland Extension — Blossom End Rot of Vegetables

lessons.title: Blossom end rot: a water problem, not a soil problem
body: Blossom end rot is a dark, sunken spot on the bottom of a fruit. It hits tomatoes most, but also peppers, eggplant, squash, and melons. Big slicing and paste tomatoes get it more than cherry tomatoes. It often shows up on the first fruits of the year. In Australia and other southern places, that means spring fruit in about October and November.
The cause is too little calcium inside the growing fruit. But most of the time the soil has plenty of calcium. The problem is getting it into the fruit.

Here is why. Calcium rides up the plant in water. Water flows to the parts that lose the most of it to the air. Leaves lose a lot of water. Fruits lose very little. So most calcium goes to the leaves, and it stays there. It does not move back out to the fruit later.

Many things slow that flow. Dry spells, or wet and dry swings, slow it. So do soggy or cold soil and cut roots. Hot, windy days and very humid days can slow it too. Too much nitrogen makes lots of leaves, and they pull even more calcium away from fruit. Too much potassium, magnesium, or salt in the soil can block calcium.

This is why extra lime or calcium often does not help. Lime can also push soil pH too high. Fix the water first. Water deeply and on a regular schedule. Mulch to keep the soil evenly moist. Don't dig within a foot of the stem. Go easy on nitrogen. Test your soil before you add calcium. Pick off spotted fruit, and try a different variety if one keeps getting it.
lessons.tip: Push a finger into the soil every day or two. Water when it feels dry an inch down, so it never swings from dust to mud.

quiz.q: Why do leaves get more calcium than fruits?
options: Calcium moves with water, and leaves lose more water
Bees eat the calcium in fruit

sources.t: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook — Chapter 3: Botany

lessons.title: Photosynthesis: how plants make food from light
body: Animals eat to get food. Plants make their own. They do it with light, water, and a gas in the air called carbon dioxide. This is called photosynthesis (say foe-toe-SIN-thuh-sis). The word means "put together with light."

It happens in tiny parts of leaf cells called chloroplasts. They hold a green color called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll catches light energy. The plant uses that energy to join carbon dioxide and water into sugar. Oxygen is left over and goes out into the air. In short: carbon dioxide plus water plus light makes sugar plus oxygen.

Leaves are built for this job. They are flat and wide to catch light. Carbon dioxide gets in through tiny holes called stomata. When the plant is short on water, those holes close. Then photosynthesis slows or stops.
Light matters in three ways. How bright it is. How long it lasts each day. And its color. Red and blue light work best. Plants bounce most green light away. That is why they look green to us.
Heat matters too. Most plants make food fastest from about 65 to 85°F. Above or below that, it slows down.

Sugar is not just food to burn. A second process, respiration, breaks sugar down to release energy. It happens in all living cells, day and night. Photosynthesis builds up stored energy. Respiration lets it out. A plant grows when it makes more sugar than it uses.
lessons.tip: Grow fruiting crops where they get full sun. More light means more sugar for fruit.

quiz.q: What does a plant give off as a leftover when it makes sugar?

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing tomatoes in home gardens
University of Illinois Extension — Tomato

lessons.title: Grow a tomato plant
body: Tomatoes love heat and sun. Frost can kill them. So plant them outside only after the last frost, when the soil feels warm.
Most people start with a small plant, not a seed. Pick a short, sturdy plant with green leaves. Give it a spot with full sun.
Put in a stake or a cage on planting day. The plant will grow tall and floppy. The cage holds it up later.
Water the soil, not the leaves. Try to keep the soil damp all the time, not dry one day and soaked the next. Pick tomatoes when they are full color but still firm.
lessons.tip: Ask an adult to help push the cage in. Do it right away, so you don't hurt big roots later.

quiz.q: When should you put a cage by your tomato plant?

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing carrots and parsnips in home gardens
University of Maryland Extension — Growing Carrots in a Home Garden

lessons.title: Grow straight carrots
body: A carrot is a root. It pushes straight down into the dirt. If it hits a rock or hard clumps, it can bend or split in two.
So first, dig the soil deep and loose. Pull out rocks and sticks. A raised bed works great.
Plant the tiny seeds right in the garden, not in pots. Cover them with a thin layer of soil. Keep the top damp. The seeds can take up to three weeks to sprout!
When the plants are a few inches tall, thin them. Leave about two to four inches between each one. Then each carrot has room to grow fat.
lessons.tip: Mix a few radish seeds in the row. They pop up fast and show you where the carrots are.

quiz.q: What can make a carrot grow bent or split?

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing strawberries in the home garden

lessons.title: Start a strawberry patch
body: Strawberries need lots of sun. Give them at least six hours a day. More is better.
Set the plants about a foot or more apart. They will spread. Each plant sends out long stems called runners. A runner grows a new baby plant at its tip.
Here is a hard but smart job. For the first few weeks after planting, pinch off the flowers. This lets the plant grow strong roots and leaves first. Then it can make more fruit later.
Bees help make the berries. Pick berries when they are red all over. Pick often, so bugs don't get them first.
lessons.tip: Snip off some runners as they grow. If you don't, your patch can take over the yard!

quiz.q: Why pinch off a new plant's first flowers?
options: So the plant grows roots and leaves first

sources.t: University of Minnesota Extension — Cucumber beetles
University of Delaware Cooperative Extension — Non-chemical pest control for cucurbits

lessons.title: Stop cucumber beetles
body: Cucumber beetles are small yellow bugs. One kind has three black stripes. The other kind has twelve black spots. They eat squash, cucumber, and melon plants. These beetles live in much of North America.
They hurt young plants the most. They chew the leaves and flowers. Worse, the striped kind can carry a germ that causes bacterial wilt. Wilt makes cucumbers and melons droop and die.

Here is how to stop them. Cover young plants with a light cloth called a row cover. Take it off when flowers open, so bees can reach them. Once plants are bigger, spread thick straw around the stems. It makes it harder for beetles to lay eggs.
If you only have a few plants, knock the beetles into a bucket of soapy water. Yellow sticky traps can catch them too. In fall, clean up old vines and move these crops to a new spot next year.
lessons.tip: Check under the leaves early in the morning. The beetles are slow then, and easy to catch.

quiz.q: When should you take the row cover off?

sources.t: University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension — Composting Manure and Other Organic Materials (G1315)
UC Statewide IPM Program — Composting

lessons.title: Hot compost: how a pile cooks itself
body: A compost pile can get hot inside. Nobody lights a fire. Tiny living things called microbes make the heat. Microbes are bacteria and fungi too small to see. As they eat, they give off heat, just like your body does.

To work fast, microbes need four things. They need food, water, air, and the right mix. The mix is carbon to nitrogen. Browns like dry leaves and paper are high in carbon. Greens like grass and food scraps are high in nitrogen. Microbes like about 25 to 30 parts carbon for each part nitrogen. Mixing equal amounts of greens and browns gets close.

Size matters too. A pile about three feet on each side holds heat in the middle. A small pile loses heat too fast. The pile should feel damp, but not soggy. Too dry, and the microbes stop working. Too wet, and air can't get in, so the pile slows down.

A good hot pile stays at about 130 to 140 degrees F. Heat that high kills many germs. It takes about 145 degrees to kill weed seeds. But if it gets much hotter, the microbes start to die. Guides say to turn it once it climbs past about 145 to 160 degrees. A long compost thermometer shows you what is going on inside.
Turning stirs in fresh air. Turn the pile when it gets too hot, or when it cools below about 104 degrees. When turning no longer heats it back up, let it rest for a month or more. Then it is done.
lessons.tip: Ask an adult to help turn a big pile with a fork. Wear gloves, and wash your hands after.

quiz.q: What makes the heat in a compost pile?

sources.t: Virginia Cooperative Extension — What are Indoor Vertical Farms? (SPES-818)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 1): Farms that grow up
body: Most farms spread out flat on the land. A vertical farm grows plants in layers, stacked one on top of another. It is like a tall shelf full of plants.
Many vertical farms are inside buildings. People control the light, the heat, and the air. The plants do not need soil. Their roots get water with plant food mixed in.
This lets people grow fresh food all year, even in a big city. It uses less water than many farms. But the lights cost a lot of money to run.
lessons.tip: A shelf of plants under a grow light at home is a tiny vertical farm. Ask an adult to set up the light.

quiz.q: How does a vertical farm grow plants?

sources.t: UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County — Vertical Hydroponic Towers
Oklahoma State University Extension — Building a Vertical Hydroponic Tower (HLA-6724)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 2): What a grow tower is
body: A grow tower is a tall tube with holes up and down its sides. A small plant sits in each hole. Lots of plants fit in a small space, like a patio or a balcony.
At the bottom is a tank of water with plant food in it. A pump pushes the water up to the top. Then it trickles down inside the tower, past the roots. It drips back into the tank.
The same water goes around again and again, so very little is wasted. Lettuce, herbs, and strawberries grow well in towers.
lessons.tip: Outside, a tower needs a sunny spot. Inside, it needs a grow light.

quiz.q: Where does the water go after it trickles down a grow tower?

sources.t: Oklahoma State University Extension — Building a Vertical Hydroponic Tower (HLA-6724)
UF/IFAS Extension — Production Systems, Florida Greenhouse Vegetable Production Handbook (CV263)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 3): Set up a tower
body: Pick the spot first. The tank holds a lot of water, so a full tower is heavy and hard to move. One home tower plan uses a tank that holds about 170 liters (45 gallons). Outside, pick a sunny spot. Inside, plan for a grow light over the tower.

Think about height. A tower about 1.5 to 1.8 meters (5 to 6 feet) tall is easy for most people to reach. Leave space between towers, too. Tall towers set close together shade the plants near the bottom. Some towers can turn, so each side gets its share of sun.
Use food-safe parts, since you will eat what grows. The lid on the tank should block light. Light on the water lets green algae grow. Tie the top of a tall tower to something strong so it can't tip.
Outside, towers get cold fast. They stand up high, away from the warm ground. When frost is coming, cover them or move them under shelter.
lessons.tip: Water and electricity do not mix. Have an adult plug in the pump and keep the cord and plug dry.

quiz.q: Why should the lid on a tower's tank block light?
options: To help the pump run faster

sources.t: Oklahoma State University Extension — Building a Vertical Hydroponic Tower (HLA-6724)
UF/IFAS Extension — Growing Lettuce in Small Hydroponic Systems (HS1422)
Virginia Cooperative Extension — What are Indoor Vertical Farms? (SPES-818)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 4): Water and plant food
body: In a tower, the roots get all their food from the water. So use a plant food made for hydroponics, which means growing without soil.

A timer turns the pump on and off. The best timing depends on the crop. In one university tower guide, lettuce got water all day and night. Strawberries got water 7 to 10 times a day, for one hour each time.
Check the tank often. Plants drink every day, so keep the water at the right level. Test the water with pH and EC meters, too. To learn how, see the lesson "Hydroponic nutrient solution: pH and EC."
Keep the water from getting too hot or too cold. For lettuce, about 18 to 27°C (65 to 80°F) is a good range.
Watch out if the power goes off. With no pump, the water stops. Roots can dry out fast. Look at the tower each day to make sure water is flowing.
lessons.tip: An adult should mix the plant food and any pH up or pH down, wearing gloves.

quiz.q: What turns a tower's pump on and off?

sources.t: Oklahoma State University Extension — Building a Vertical Hydroponic Tower (HLA-6724)
UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County — Vertical Hydroponic Towers
UF/IFAS Extension — Growing Lettuce in Small Hydroponic Systems (HS1422)
Virginia Cooperative Extension — What are Indoor Vertical Farms? (SPES-818)
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Hydroponic Production of Edible Crops: Management Basics (SPES-462)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 5): Best crops for a tower
body: Towers work best for small plants that grow fast. Leafy greens like lettuce, spinach, kale, and Swiss chard are great picks. So are herbs like basil and cilantro. Strawberries do well, too.
Fast crops are easier. Lettuce can be ready in about 50 to 60 days. Plants that take longer than that are harder to grow in small water gardens.

Give each plant room. One tower guide spaces leaf lettuce 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches) apart. Head lettuce, spinach, kale, and strawberries get about 30 cm (12 inches). Broccoli needs about 45 cm (18 inches).

Skip big, heavy plants. Tall tomatoes, peppers, and vining cucumbers need lots of root room and a trellis to hold them up. Fruit crops also need more light and more time than greens. If you want to try one, pick a small or dwarf kind, like a dwarf tomato.
lessons.tip: The bottom of a tower gets less light. If the low plants grow slowly, turn the tower so each side gets a turn in the light.

quiz.q: Which crop is a good pick for a grow tower?

sources.t: Virginia Cooperative Extension — Hydroponic Production of Edible Crops: Management Basics (SPES-462)
South Dakota State University Extension — Small-scale Hydroponic Production Systems (P-00337)
UF/IFAS Extension — Growing Lettuce in Small Hydroponic Systems (HS1422)
Virginia Cooperative Extension — What are Indoor Vertical Farms? (SPES-818)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 6): Light for indoor towers
body: Plants use light to make their food. Indoors, the grow light is their only sun. To learn how leaves turn light into food, see the lesson "Photosynthesis: how plants make food from light."

Two things set how much light a plant gets. One is how bright the light is. The other is how many hours it stays on. Growers add them up into one number for the whole day. It is called the daily light integral, or DLI. Think of it as a bucket that fills with light all day.

Lettuce grows best with a DLI of about 17. A clear summer day outside gives more than twice that. Winter days give much less. For leafy greens, a good rule is that 1% more light gives about 1% more growth. But too much light can burn the leaf edges. This is called tip burn.
Hours count, too. Leafy greens do well with 12 to 16 hours of light a day. Plants grown for fruit may need up to 18 hours. Too many hours can stunt plants and twist their leaves.

Distance counts. A light too close can burn young leaves. A light too far makes plants tall, thin, and weak. Raise the light as the plants grow. Towers have one more problem. The bottom gets less light than the top. Growers fix this by turning the tower or by hanging light strips along its sides.
lessons.tip: Put the grow light on a timer, so the plants get the same hours each day.

quiz.q: What does DLI measure?
options: All the light a plant gets in one day
How much water a plant drinks

sources.t: University of Kentucky / e-GRO — Root Disease Management in Hydroponic Systems
Colorado State University Extension PlantTalk — Root Disease Problems and Management in Hydroponic Systems
Oklahoma State University Extension — Building a Vertical Hydroponic Tower (HLA-6724)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 7): Keep a tower clean
body: The worst problem in water gardens is root rot. It is most often caused by Pythium (say pih-THEE-um). It is a water mold, not a true fungus. Its tiny spores can swim through water to find hurt root tips.
Healthy roots are white. Sick roots turn brown and soft. The first sign you see above is often wilting or brown leaf tips. Take sick plants out right away, so the mold does not spread.
Pythium lives in soil. It can sneak in on dirty tools, shoes, or plants. Warm water with little air helps it grow. Cool water helps slow it. About 20 to 22°C (68 to 72°F) is best for lettuce roots.

Algae is the green slime that grows where light hits water. It slows plant growth. It also feeds small flies, like fungus gnats and shore flies. These flies can carry root rot spores. So keep light out of the tank and the tower.
Clean the whole tower after each crop. First scrub off old roots and slime. Then kill germs with a cleaner like a weak bleach mix. Follow the label.
lessons.tip: Only an adult should mix and use bleach, with gloves on and windows open.

quiz.q: What color are healthy roots in a grow tower?

sources.t: USDA NIFA — Optimizing the Cost-Effectiveness of Lighting in Controlled Environment Agriculture
USDA NIFA — Saving, Reducing, and Offsetting Energy for Indoor Specialty-Crop Production (Purdue)
USDA Economic Research Service — Trends, Insights, and Future Prospects for Controlled Environment Agriculture (EIB-264)
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Hydroponic Production of Edible Crops: Management Basics (SPES-462)
Virginia Cooperative Extension — What are Indoor Vertical Farms? (SPES-818)

lessons.title: Vertical farming (Part 8): Energy and cost
body: A vertical farm trades free sunlight for electric light. That one trade shapes all of its costs. To see why, follow the energy.

An indoor farm lit only by lamps is called a plant factory. There, electric light is the biggest day-to-day cost. One USDA-funded project put lighting at about half of those costs. In a greenhouse, the sun does most of the work. Extra lamps there make up about 20 to 30 percent of the costs.

Lamps also make heat. In a closed room, that heat must be pumped out with air conditioning. Plants also let off water from their leaves, so the air must be dried, too. So the power bill grows twice: once for light, and again to take out the heat and damp.

LED lights help a lot. They cost more to buy, but they use less power and last longer. They also stay cool enough to hang close over stacked shelves. Even so, a USDA report says growing many vegetables and grains indoors still costs too much. One study found the energy to grow wheat indoors would cost about 100 times what the wheat sells for.
That is why most indoor farms grow leafy greens and herbs. These crops grow fast, stay small, and sell well. Fruit crops need more light and more time, so they use more power.
Stacking has a catch, too. In one study, lettuce yield per bit of floor was about 14 times higher in a vertical system. But the plants were packed 20 times closer. So each plant made less.

Indoor farms have real pluses. They use less water and fertilizer. They grow food all year near cities, so it travels less. They guard crops from bad weather and some pests. But they cost a lot to start, and a power failure can hurt a crop fast. Some vertical farms have closed. Experts say a farm must match its size, crops, and power costs to what buyers want.
lessons.tip: At home, use LED grow lights on a timer. Plants get the hours they need, and no power is wasted.

quiz.q: In a plant factory, what is usually the biggest day-to-day cost?

sources.t: US EPA — Composting at Home
Univ. of Maryland Extension — How to Make Compost at Home

lessons.title: Compost (Part 1): What compost is
body: Compost is a dark, crumbly soil helper. Gardeners make it from plant leftovers, like food scraps and yard trimmings.
Nature already does this work on a forest floor. Fallen leaves slowly break down and feed the ground. A compost pile does the same thing, but in a spot you choose.
Tiny living things called microbes do the breaking down. They need air and a little dampness. When the work is done, you cannot see the old scraps. You just have compost for your garden soil.
lessons.tip: Finished compost smells like wet woods or fresh dirt, not like trash.

lessons.title: Compost (Part 2): Greens and browns
body: A compost pile needs two kinds of leftovers. People call them greens and browns. The names are about what is inside, not just the color.
Greens are often wet and fresh. Fruit and veggie scraps, grass clippings, and coffee grounds are greens. They bring a plant food called nitrogen. That helps the tiny living things grow fast.
Browns are often dry. Fallen leaves, twigs, straw, and plain paper or cardboard are browns. They bring carbon, which is food energy, and they help air move through the pile.
Add about two or three scoops of browns for each scoop of greens. Always cover food scraps with a layer of browns.
lessons.tip: If your pile looks wet and heavy, add more dry leaves or torn paper.

quiz.q: Which mix is best for a compost pile?
options: Two or three parts browns for each part greens

lessons.title: Compost (Part 3): How to make compost
body: Pick a spot that drains well and is close to water. Shade helps the pile stay damp. You can use an open heap or a bin. A bin is not required.
Start with a layer of twigs or wood chips about 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 inches) thick. This lets air in at the bottom. Then add greens and browns. Chop big pieces so they break down faster.
Keep the pile as damp as a sponge you just squeezed. Turn it now and then with a fork so air can get in. Bury food scraps under dry leaves so pests stay away.
lessons.tip: A pile about 1 meter (3 feet) wide and tall holds heat better than a tiny heap.

quiz.q: How damp should a compost pile feel?
options: Like a sponge you just squeezed

lessons.title: Compost (Part 4): Why compost helps
body: Compost is a soil helper, not a full plant food by itself. Its biggest gift is better soil. Plants may still need other food if a soil test says so.

In heavy clay, compost helps the soil form crumbs. That lets air and water in, and roots can push through more easily. In sandy soil, compost helps the ground hold water and plant food so they do not wash away so fast.

Compost also feeds tiny living things in the soil. It lets out plant food slowly, a little at a time. That can mean less plant food washed into streams. Some compost even helps plants fight a few soil diseases.
Making compost has another plus. Food scraps and yard trimmings become something useful, instead of being thrown away. You get a free soil helper, and your garden can grow better.
lessons.tip: For how much compost to mix into a bed, see the lesson Soil amendments: how much compost to add.

quiz.q: What is the biggest gift compost gives the garden?
options: It replaces all plant food forever
It makes the soil itself better

lessons.title: Compost (Part 5): Piles, bins, and tumblers
body: You do not need a bin to make compost. An open pile on the ground is the simplest way. It costs little and can hold a lot of leaves and garden scraps. But a heap can dry out, look messy, and be easier for pests to reach.

A bin or box holds the pile in place. It can be wood, pallets, wire, or blocks, with gaps so air can move. A bin looks neater. It also helps hold heat and moisture, and it can keep animals out better than a bare heap.

A tumbler is a drum or barrel you can turn. Turning is easy, and the closed drum helps keep pests out. Tumblers fit small yards or patios. They hold less, though. Small ones may not stay as warm as a big pile. They work best when you fill them in one batch, then let that batch finish.
A worm bin is a different kind of box. Worms, not heat, do most of the work. It can sit indoors and needs only a little space. The next lessons show how worm bins and worm beds work.
lessons.tip: Pick the style that fits your space. A tidy bin is often best if you have close neighbors.

quiz.q: What is one plus of a compost tumbler?
options: It holds more than a big open pile
It must sit in a deep hole
It is easy to turn and helps keep pests out

lessons.title: Compost (Part 6): Compost mistakes to skip
body: Some leftovers do not belong in a home compost pile. Keep out meat, fish, bones, cheese, milk, and greasy or oily food. These can smell bad and draw rats, dogs, and flies. Also keep out dog and cat waste. It can carry germs that you do not want in garden soil.

Do not dump in only wet food or only fresh grass. That mix packs down and goes sour. Always add plenty of dry browns, and bury food scraps under leaves or paper. A pile that is all greens is one of the most common mistakes.

Skip big amounts of lime. It can turn nitrogen into a gas that smells like ammonia, and then the pile loses plant food. Leave out plants that are very sick, and weeds that have already made seed, unless you are sure the pile gets hot all the way through.

A tiny heap loses heat and dries out fast. So does a pile that you never water. Start with enough leftovers, keep the mix damp, and give it air. For how a hot pile works, see the lesson Hot compost: how a pile cooks itself.
lessons.tip: If you would not want an animal to dig for it, do not put it in the pile.

lessons.title: Compost (Part 7): Fix a compost pile
body: The tiny living things in a pile need air, water, and a mix of greens and browns. When one of those is off, the pile tells you. A rotten-egg or sour smell often means the pile is too wet or too tight. Water has filled the air spaces, so the microbes that need air cannot work well. Turn the pile and mix in dry leaves, straw, or paper. A sharp ammonia smell means too many greens. Add browns and turn it.

If the pile is soggy, you can also cover it in heavy rain so more water does not soak in. If it is too dry, the microbes slow down or stop. The middle feels dusty, and little changes. Sprinkle water as you turn, until a handful feels damp and gives up just a drop or two.

A pile that never warms up is often too small, too dry, or short on greens. Build it to about 1 meter (3 feet) on each side so the middle can hold heat. Mix in fresh grass or food scraps, add water if it is dry, and turn it. For more on how a pile heats itself, see the lesson Hot compost: how a pile cooks itself.

Pests show up when food sits on top, or when meat, dairy, or oily food went in. Take those foods out. Bury fresh scraps under a thick layer of browns. A lid, or a bin with no gaps bigger than about 6 mm (1/4 inch), helps keep animals out.
lessons.tip: Check three things first: Is it too wet, too dry, or short on browns or greens? Fix that, then wait a few days.

quiz.q: A compost pile smells like rotten eggs. What should you do first?
options: Add more food scraps and water
Turn it and mix in dry browns
Add meat to feed the microbes

lessons.title: Compost (Part 8): When compost is ready
body: Compost is ready when it is dark and crumbly, like loose soil. It should smell like wet woods or fresh earth, not like ammonia or rotten food. You should not be able to name the old scraps. A few tough bits, like twigs, are fine. You can sift those out and toss them back into a new pile.

A finished pile also stays cool. After you mix it, it should not heat up again. Then let it rest for at least a few weeks before you use it. This rest is called curing. It gives the last acids time to fade, so the compost is gentler on plants.

Mix only finished compost into garden soil. Compost that is still raw can steal nitrogen from roots as it keeps breaking down, and plants may turn yellow. As a mulch, you can spread a layer about 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 inches) thick on top of the soil, a few centimeters (a few inches) away from plant stems.

For pots, use only finished compost, and do not fill a pot with compost alone. Mix it with other potting stuff so water can drain. Compost should be no more than about one-fourth of the mix. For how much to add to a garden bed, see the lesson Soil amendments: how much compost to add.
lessons.tip: If you are not sure it is done, use it as mulch on top of the soil, not mixed around roots.

quiz.q: How can you tell compost is ready to mix into soil?
options: It is still hot and full of visible food scraps
It is dark and crumbly, smells like earth, and stays cool

lessons.title: Compost (Part 9): What a worm bin is
body: A worm bin is a closed box where worms turn food scraps into rich worm compost. People also call this vermicomposting. The worms and tiny living things do the work. The bin does not need to get hot like a compost pile. In fact, too much heat can hurt the worms.

A worm bin can sit indoors or in a shady spot outside. It takes little space, so it is a good choice if you have no yard, or if you want to compost kitchen scraps in a small home. If you care for it well, it should not smell bad or draw pests.

You need four things: a dark bin with a tight lid and air holes, damp bedding, the right worms, and food scraps. Use red wigglers, not worms from the garden or a bait shop. Garden worms do not do well in a bin.

Bury each feeding under a layer of bedding. Wait until most of the last scraps are gone before you add more. The next lessons show how to set up a larger worm bed, and how to harvest the worm compost.
lessons.tip: A worm bin is for cool, damp work. Do not add worms to a hot compost pile. The heat can kill them.

quiz.q: Which worms belong in a worm bin?
options: Any worms dug up from the garden

lessons.title: Compost (Part 10): Set up a worm bed
body: A worm bed is a larger home for composting worms than a kitchen bin. Use it when you want more worms or more scraps. Build it from plain wood, bricks, or blocks. Skip cedar and redwood, which can harm worms. A handy size is about 90 to 120 cm (3 to 4 feet) wide, at least 2.5 m (8 feet) long, and 30 to 60 cm (12 to 24 inches) deep.

Stock the bed with red wigglers (Eisenia fetida), the same worms used in bins. Do not use garden nightcrawlers. They need deep burrows and do poorly in a shallow bed. Skip jumping worms, which can hurt soil in some places.

Fill the bed with loose, damp bedding about 15 cm (6 inches) deep. Shredded paper, cardboard, old leaves, or coconut coir all work. Keep the top 10 cm (4 inches) moist and crumbly, not soggy. Worms breathe through their skin, so they need that dampness, but standing water leaves them with no air.

Keep the bed in shade or under a roof. Red wigglers live and breed from about 13 to 29°C (55 to 85°F). They work best around 16 to 27°C (60 to 80°F). In harsh heat or cold, a bed sunk 30 to 60 cm (12 to 24 inches) into the ground stays more even.
Feed fruit and veggie scraps only after the last food is gone. Keep out meat, dairy, oily food, lots of citrus or onion, and pet waste. Do not turn a worm bed like a compost pile.
lessons.tip: If you are not sure a new food is safe, try a small amount with a few worms first and watch them for a day.

quiz.q: What kind of worms should you put in a worm bed?

lessons.title: Compost (Part 11): Harvest worm castings
body: Worm castings are the dark, crumbly waste that worms leave behind. Worm compost is a mix of those castings plus leftover bedding and bits of food. After a few months, the bin or bed looks more like fine soil than paper and scraps. That is the time to harvest.

You need to separate the worms from this finished stuff. A thick layer of castings is not healthy for them. One easy way is to push the old material to one side and add fresh, damp bedding and food on the empty side. Over two to three weeks, most worms move to the new food. Then lift out the finished compost. You can also spread the contents in a bright room. Worms crawl down from the light, and you scoop off the top a little at a time.

Worm compost can be used right away, or stored in a bag with a few air holes. Mix it into garden soil, or sprinkle a thin layer on top of the soil around plants. Keep it out of harsh sun, or cover it with mulch. In a potting mix, use no more than about one-fourth worm compost. Pure castings can be a bit salty, so use them lightly, and keep them off the roots of tiny seedlings.

When a bed gets crowded, split it. Move some worms, plus some of their bedding, into a second bed of fresh, damp bedding. Put any little lemon-shaped cocoons you see back with the worms so the babies can hatch.
lessons.tip: Look for shiny, light-brown cocoons about the size of a match head, and tuck them back into the fresh bedding.

quiz.q: Why do you separate worms from finished castings?
options: Castings are unsafe for people to touch
Worms cannot live without food scraps on top
Too many castings are unhealthy for the worms

lessons.title: Structures (Part 1): What garden structures are
body: A garden structure is something you build or set up to help the garden, or to help you work in it. It is not a plant. It is a tool that stays in place.
Some structures help plants climb, like a trellis. Some keep tools dry, like a shed. Some trap the sun's warmth, like a cold frame or a hoop house. Each one does a different job.

Pick a structure by the job you need most, the space you have, and what you can care for. A small start is fine. Before you put up a shed or a hoop house, ask about local building rules. Some places need a permit.
lessons.tip: Walk your garden first. Note sun, slope, and how you move tools. Then choose a structure that fits that spot.

quiz.q: What should you think about first when you pick a garden structure?
options: The job you need it to do
Buying the biggest one you see

lessons.title: Structures (Part 2): What a trellis is
body: A trellis is a frame that helps climbing plants grow up, not across the ground. It can be wood, metal, or posts with netting or wire between them.
Put the trellis in when you plant. If you pound posts in later, you can hurt roots and stems. Set the posts deep, so wind cannot tip the frame when the vines get heavy.

The next lesson shows different kinds of supports, and how to train and tie vines. For which crops climb on their own, and which need a cage or a tie, see the lesson Grow up: trellises, stakes, and cages.
lessons.tip: A wobbly trellis will fall when fruit gets heavy. Test it with a firm push before you plant.

quiz.q: When should you put a trellis in the ground?
options: After the vines are already long
When you plant, so you do not hurt roots later

lessons.title: Structures (Part 3): Vine supports and training
body: Supports come in several shapes. A flat, upright trellis is two strong posts with mesh or netting stretched between them. Pound the posts deep so wind cannot tip them. Use stronger mesh for heavy vines. An A-frame looks like a tall letter A, and vines climb both sides.

Stiff farm wire panels can be bent or joined into an arch over a path. Push the bottom wires into the soil so the arch stays put. You can walk under it to pick. Stakes and cages help plants that do not grab on their own, like many tomatoes. Set them on planting day. Small store cages can be too short for tall plants. Use a sturdy cage and two stakes. See Grow up: trellises, stakes, and cages for which crops need tying.

As vines grow, gently weave the tips through the mesh every few days. When you must tie a stem, use soft cloth or stretchy ties, not thin wire that can cut. Make a loose loop like a figure 8. One loop holds the post, and one holds the stem. Leave room for the stem to thicken. Add a new tie about every 30 cm (12 inches) as the plant grows.

Heavy fruit, like many melons, may drop when ripe. When the fruit is still small, tie a wide cloth strip to the support so the middle hangs like a little hammock. Then set the fruit in it. Small cucumbers often do not need a sling. Very large pumpkins are too heavy to hang. Grow those on the ground.
lessons.tip: Check the ties after a windy day. If a tie is tight on the stem, loosen it.

quiz.q: How should you tie a vine to a stake?
options: With a loose, soft figure-8 tie that leaves room for the stem to grow
With no tie, even if the plant cannot grab on

lessons.title: Structures (Part 4): Garden sheds
body: A garden shed is a small building for tools, pots, and supplies. Its most important jobs are to stay dry and to keep things safe. Place it close to the garden, on ground that drains well, and where you can reach it easily. A little shade helps it stay cooler. A ramp is easier than steps when you roll a cart or a wheelbarrow.

The shed needs a sound roof so rain and snow cannot leak in. Paint or seal the sides to protect them. Vents help hot air and smells escape, which matters if you store fuels or strong fertilizers. An adult should store those in a safe, aired cabinet. Strong hinges, a good latch, and shelves or hooks on the walls make the shed easier to use.

Building rules are not the same everywhere. Some places ask for a permit even for a small or portable shed. There may be rules about how far a shed can sit from a property line, or how many extra buildings you may have. Check with your local planning office before you buy or build. If you skip this step, you might have to move the shed, or even take it down.
lessons.tip: Keep the floor dry and the door easy to open. After a storm, look for leaks and loose parts.

quiz.q: What should you do before you put up a garden shed?
options: Paint it first, then pick a spot later
Check local building or planning rules
Set it in the lowest, wettest part of the yard

lessons.title: Structures (Part 5): Hoop houses and tunnels
body: A hoop house is a walk-in set of hoops with clear plastic over them. People also call it a plastic tunnel. The sun warms the air inside. Many hoop houses have no heater and no fans. You let heat out by rolling up the sides and opening the end doors. For vents, fans, and heaters in a true greenhouse, see the lessons What a greenhouse does and Greenhouse air: letting heat out and keeping it in.

A hoop house can make the growing time longer. It can also shield plants from wind and frost. On a sunny day it can get much hotter than the open garden. The jump can be about 11 to 22°C (20 to 40°F). Open it when it warms up. Close the sides when the wind is strong, so the plastic does not rip.

Pick a flat spot that drains well. It needs plenty of sun and water nearby. Keep rain from running into the tunnel. Drive the posts deep, about 60 to 75 cm (24 to 30 inches). Add extra anchors in windy places. A roof that comes to a point sheds snow better than a round roof.

Rules for hoop houses are not the same everywhere. Some places treat a plastic tunnel as a short-term building and do not ask for a permit. Other places do. Ask your local planning office before you build.
lessons.tip: Open the sides on sunny days, and close them before a hard wind or a frosty night.

quiz.q: How do you usually let heat out of a hoop house?
options: By rolling up the sides and opening the end doors

lessons.title: Structures (Part 6): Cold frames
body: A cold frame is a low box with a clear, sloping lid. It traps a little of the sun's warmth and blocks wind. It is not a walk-in house. You work by lifting the lid. For how a cold frame compares with row covers, see the lesson Stretch the season: row covers and cold frames.

Set the box on ground that drains well, close to water, and in a spot that gets good light. Build the back wall higher than the front so the lid slopes toward the midday sun. That brings in more light, and it helps rain and snow run off. In the northern half of the world, the low side often faces south. In the southern half, it often faces north.

A closed frame can overheat on a sunny day. Prop the lid open, or take it off, and use a thermometer if you have one. Open the lid on the side away from the wind, so a gust does not flip it or burn tender leaves. Close it again later in the day, before the air cools. Water early, so leaves can dry before you shut the lid.

On very cold nights, an extra mat or blanket over the lid can hold a little more heat. Take it off when the sun returns. Lightweight frames can blow away, so hook, peg, or weigh the lid down. After a hard wind, check that the lid is still tight.
lessons.tip: Never use wood treated with creosote or similar old wood poisons for a frame. The fumes can hurt plants in a closed box.

quiz.q: What should you do with a cold frame lid on a warm, sunny day?
options: Prop it open, or take it off, so the plants do not overheat
Cover it with a thick, wet blanket

lessons.title: Structures (Part 7): Wind, snow, and storms
body: Wind and snow push on garden structures. Wind tries to lift and tip them. Loose plastic acts like a sail. It can tear, or pull a hoop house out of the ground. Snow is heavy. Wet snow weighs more than dry snow. If it piles up, it can bend hoops or crush a roof.

Good anchoring starts when you build. Drive hoop-house posts about 60 to 90 cm (2 to 3 feet) deep. In windy or sandy ground, add screw anchors or tie-downs. Space hoops no more than about 1.2 m (4 feet) apart. A pointed roof sheds snow better than a low, round one. If you can, point the ends of the tunnel toward the strongest usual winds, so the long sides catch less force. A windbreak can help, but keep it far enough that branches cannot fall on it, and the garden still gets sun.

When a big wind is coming, close and fasten hoop-house sides, ends, and doors. Bring in loose pots and tools. Keep the plastic tight. Check bolts and braces before snow arrives. If a tunnel is not built for heavy snow, an adult can take the plastic off. Posts under the ridge can help a covered tunnel hold the weight. Do not climb on the plastic. Ask an adult to clear snow.

Cold frames need their lids pegged or weighed down, because gusts often cause damage. After any storm, walk the garden. Look for torn plastic, bent frames, loose bolts, and leaks in a shed roof. Fix loose parts soon.
lessons.tip: After a storm, check structures in daylight, and keep children away until an adult says it is safe.

quiz.q: What should you do when a strong wind is on the way?
options: Close and fasten hoop-house sides and doors, and tighten loose plastic
Roll every side wide open and leave it
Poke holes in the plastic so wind can pass through
